Random dynamical systems theory and application to turbulence
PDF All research

Random dynamical systems theory and application to turbulence

Samuel Chan-ashing
Research stay · 2022 · Cambridge
PDF

We study the chaotic motion of a turbulent system for which its flow is associated to a velocity field arising from the Navier-Stokes equations in 2D and 3D. Our approach involves exploiting randomness to consider the average behaviour of the fluid, and we thus subject the fluid to white-in-time, Hs\mathrm{H}^s-in-space stochastic forcing in a periodic box.

The key features of our study are tools from ergodic theory and random dynamical systems. The Multiplicative Ergodic Theorem allows us to define the Lyapunov exponent and a new version of Furstenberg’s criterion, combined with hypoellipticity and approximate control arguments, allows us to prove the Lagrangian chaos of our system, that is, the top Lyapunov exponent is strictly positive.

1Introduction

1.1. Turbulence

In the physics and engineering literature, turbulence is used to describe a wide range of observed phenomena in dynamics of weakly dissipative, infinite dimensional and where the nonlinearity has to be of a certain type (fluids, nonlinear waves, etc). These conservative systems are described in generic settings, including both 2D and 3D incompressible or compressible Navier-Stokes, passive scalars advected by fluids, nonlinear dispersive equations, magneto-hydrodynamics models and kinetic models in plasmas.

Basic properties of turbulent systems

All turbulent system shared some basic properties that are:
Property of chaos. The system is extremely sensitive to initial data.
Observation of chaos: if we subject the system to the same force and slightly change the initial data, we then get a very different answer (for example: exponentially fast).
Property of ergodicity. Time averages the same as running multiple experiments.
Property of multiscale. The system exhibits a multitude of scales and a cascade between scales: fills out an inertial range between the injection scale and the dissipation scale(s).
This forcing generally acts at sort of one set of scales, called injection scale (or integral scale), and the energy that it puts in, spreads out among all the other scales available in the system.
Observation of multiscale: if the previous operator N\mathrm{N} acts like a laplacian then what can sometimes happen is that the injection scale put in scale one, the nonlinearity mixing everythings up and sends information from low frequencies to high frequencies where the dissipation is very strong (even if ν→0\nu\rightarrow 0 the dissipation is never vanishing).
Property of universality. Statitics between the largest and smallest scales appear to be universal, i.e., independant of details of experiment (e.g. basically independent of F\mathrm{F} and D\mathrm{D}).
Observation of universality: when we want to understand how the kinetic energy distribute itself through the inertial range we observe a graph, called the power spectrum, which is a log-log plot of the energy density as a function of frequency multiplied by kk to the dimension minus 11: E(k)=|k|p𝔼(|û(k)|2).\mathrm{E}(k) \,=\, |k|^{p} \mathbb{E}(\left|\hat{u}(k)\right|^{2}).

Property of anomalous dissipation. A constant on-average flux of conserved quantities through the inertial range.
More generally, we have the following universal law:

Observability and statistical stationarity

Consider a fluid uu. Most classical case is t→+∞t \rightarrow+\infty to statistical steady state, then focus on dissipation to zero. Thus, the equation studied has the general form: ∂tu=N[u]+νDu+F,\partial_{t} u \;\,=\,\; \mathrm{N}[u] \;+\; \nu \mathrm{D}u \;+\; \mathrm{F}, where N\mathrm{N} is an operator, ν\nu is the dissipation and F\mathrm{F} is a external diving force.
Many turbulent systems are well-approximated as statistically stationary, like wind over a sail or water over a stone. For systems in fluid mechanics, we observe that these stationary statistics do not depend on the initial data and that time averages are the same as ensemble averages.
Hence, the main idea is that there should be an invariant measure μ\mu over a phase space 𝑯\mathbf{H} such that if you randomize the initial condition (i.e., u0∼Lawμu_{0} \stackrel{\text{Law}}{\sim} \mu), then this law doesn’t change as a function of time: u0∼ Law μ⇒∀t≥0:ut∼ Law μ.u_{0} \stackrel{\text { Law }}{\sim} \mu \qquad \Longrightarrow\qquad \forall \,t \,\geqslant\,0 \;:\quad u_{t} \stackrel{\text { Law }}{\sim} \mu.

Notations 1

For f∈L1(X,μ)f\in\mathrm{L}^1(\mathrm{X},\mu), we denote: 𝔼μ(f)=∫Xf(x)μ(dx)and∥f∥Lp(X)=(𝔼(|f|p))1/p.\mathbb{E}_{\mu}(f) \,=\, \int_{\mathrm{X}} f(x) \, \mu(\mathrm{d}x) \qquad\mathrm{and}\qquad\left\|f\right\|_{\mathrm{L}^{p}(\mathrm{X})} \,=\, \left(\mathbb{E}(\left|f\right|^{p})\right)^{1/p}.

The ensemble averages of an observable φ:𝑯→𝑹\varphi: \mathbf{H}\longrightarrow\mathbf{R} is given by 𝔼μ(φ):=∫𝑯φ(u)dμ(u).\mathbb{E}_{\mu}(\varphi) \;:=\; \int_{\mathbf{H}} \varphi(u)\,\mathrm{d}\mu(u).

However, we also want that the measure is ergodic: for μ\mu-a.e. initial condition uu, limT+∞1T∫0Tφ(ut)dt=𝔼μ(φ).\lim_{\mathrm{T}+\infty} \;\frac{1}{\mathrm{T}} \int_{0}^{\mathrm{T}} \varphi(u_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t \;\,=\,\; \mathbb{E}_{\mu}(\varphi). More precisely, we want that these ergodic averages hold for generic data.

1.2. Model

Let d=2d=2 or 33. Stochastic differential equations model our real phenomenon well, because many turbulent systems are well-approximated by statistically stationary. However, the issue with this model is that for deterministic systems, the construction of the invariant measures which model this behavior is deeply challenging, even for relatively simple, finite dimensional ODEs. This provides a major first motivation for moving to random systems.

Notations 2

We use the following Fourier transform convention: f̂(k)=1(2π)d/2∫𝕋df(x)e−ik⋅xdx.\hat{f}(k) \,=\, \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{d/2}} \int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}} f(x) e^{-ik\cdot x} \,\mathrm{d}x. We consider (ek)(e_k) a real Fourier basis for functions on 𝕋d\mathbb{T}^d.
We denote f≲a,b,c,…gf \underset{a,b,c,\hdots}{\lesssim} g if there exists a constante C=C(a,b,c,…)C\,=\,C(a,b,c,\hdots) such that f≤Cgf \,\leqslant\,C g.

Phase space

The state space for our fluid velocity fields is Hs\mathrm{H}^s, the Sobolev space of mappings with regularity ss, with mean zero divergence free: 𝑯:={u∈Hs(𝕋d,𝑹d):∇⋅u=0and∫𝕋du=0}.\mathbf{H}\;:=\; \left\{u \in \mathrm{H}^s(\mathbb{T}^d, \mathbf{R}^d) \;:\quad \nabla\cdot u \,=\, 0\quad \text{and} \quad \int_{\mathbb{T}^d} u \,=\, 0\right\}. We write: ∥f∥Hs=∑k∈𝒁d|k|2s|f̂(k)|2\quad\displaystyle\left\|f\right\|_{\mathrm{H}^{s}} \,=\, \sum_{k \in \mathbf{Z}^{d}} \left|k\right|^{2 s}|\hat{f}(k)|^{2}.

Fluid mechanics models

We consider fluid mechanics subject to white-in-time, Hs\mathrm{H}^s-in-space stochastic forcing in a periodic box 𝕋d(d=2,3)\mathbb{T}^d \; (d=2,3) which is non-degenerate at high frequencies. We adopt an approach that considers the average behavior of fluids across all turbulent systems: the fluid velocity evolves according to a time-continuous, randomly driven ergodic motion. Then, let ut:𝕋d→𝑹du_t : \mathbb{T}^d \longrightarrow\mathbf{R}^d be the random velocity field at time t>0t\,>\,0 which evolves according to one of several incompressible, stochastically forced fluid mechanics models:
System 1. 2D Navier-Stokes system in 𝕋2\mathbb{T}^2. This SPDE is: {∂tut+ut⋅∇ut=−∇pt+νΔut+QẆt , ∇⋅ut=0 , u0∈𝑯 . \begin{cases} \partial_t u_t + u_t\cdot\nabla u_t\,=\, -\nabla p_t + \nu\Delta u_t + Q \dot{W}_t \text{ , } \\ \nabla \cdot u_t \,=\, 0 \text{ , } \\ u_0 \in \mathbf{H}\text{ . } \end{cases}

System 2. 3D hyper-viscous Navier-Stokes system in 𝕋3\mathbb{T}^3. This SPDE is: {∂tut+ut⋅∇ut=−∇pt+νΔut−ηΔ2ut+QẆt , ∇⋅ut=0 , u0∈𝑯 . \begin{cases} \partial_t u_t + u_t\cdot\nabla u_t\,=\, -\nabla p_t + \nu\Delta u_t -\eta\Delta^2u_t+ Q \dot{W}_t \text{ , } \\ \nabla \cdot u_t \,=\, 0 \text{ , } \\ u_0 \in \mathbf{H}\text{ . } \end{cases} where:

  • WtW_{t}: is a cylindrical Wiener process on 𝑯\mathbf{H} defined by Wt:=∑m∈𝒁d∖{0}emγmWtm,W_{t} \;:=\; \sum_{m \in \mathbf{Z}^d\backslash\{0\}} e_{m} \gamma_m W_{t}^{m}, where (Wtm)m(W_{t}^{m})_m is a family of independent (d−1)(d-1)-dimensional Wiener processes on a common canonical filtered probability space (Ω,ℱ,(ℱt),ℙ)(\Omega, \mathcal{F},(\mathcal{F}_{t}), \mathbb{P}).

  • QQ: is a positive Hilbert-Schmidt operator on mean-zero, divergence free L2\mathrm{L}^{2} vector fields with singular values (qk)k∈𝒁d∖{0}(q_k)_{k\in\mathbf{Z}^d\backslash\{0\}} satisfying: qk≈|k|−α,q_{k}\;\approx\;\left|k\right|^{-\alpha}, for an arbitrary, fixed α>5d/2\alpha\,>\,5d/2. This condition says that the forcing is supported in every mode (we can also only consider the case of high frequencies qk≳|k|−αq_{k}\;\gtrsim\;\left|k\right|^{-\alpha}).

For the remainder of this article, we take s∈(α−2(d−1),α−d2)s \in \left(\alpha-2(d-1), \,\alpha-\frac{d}{2}\right) and thus s>d2+3s\,>\,\frac{d}{2}+3, which implies that the velocities are always at least 𝒞3\mathcal{C}^{3} in space: 𝑯↪𝒞3.\mathbf{H}\;\hookrightarrow\; \mathcal{C}^{3}.

Almost-sure global well-posedness

Let’s re-write the Navier-Stokes system as an evolution equation on 𝑯\mathbf{H}: ∂tu+B(u,u)+Au=QẆ=∑m∈𝒁d∖{0}qmemẆm,\partial_{t} u + \mathrm{B}(u, u) + \mathrm{A}u \;\,=\,\; Q \dot{W} \;\,=\,\; \sum_{m \in \mathbf{Z}^d\backslash\{0\}} q_{m} e_{m} \dot{W}^{m}, where the Euler nonlinearity in both 2D and 3D is denoted by:

  • B(u,v)=∇⋅p(u⊗v)\mathrm{B}(u, v) \,=\, \nabla \cdot p(u \otimes v),

  • p=(id−∇(−Δ)−1∇⋅)p \,=\, (\mathrm{id}-\nabla(-\Delta)^{-1} \nabla \cdot) is the Leray projection,

  • Au={−νΔu if d=2 , −νΔu+ηΔ2u if d=3 . \displaystyle\mathrm{A}u \,=\, \begin{cases} -\nu \Delta u & \text{ if } d\,=\,2 \text{ , } \\ -\nu \Delta u + \eta \Delta^{2} u & \text{ if } d\,=\,3 \text{ . } \end{cases} is the dissipation operator.

Remark

Note that: e−tAe^{-t\mathrm{A}} is the propagator of the heat semigroup in 2D, and η\eta is the hyperviscosity in 3D.

We follow the standard procedure of defining the (ut)(u_t) process to be a solution of equation in the mild sens, i.e.,

Proposition 1 (Mild formulation)

The (ut)(u_{t}) process with initial data uu is a solution of: ut=e−tAu+Γt+∫0te−(t−s)AB(us,us)ds,u_{t} \,=\, e^{-t \mathrm{A}} u + \Gamma_t + \int_{0}^{t} e^{-(t-s) \mathrm{A}} \mathrm{B}(u_{s}, u_{s}) \,\mathrm{d}s, where Γt=∫0te−(t−s)AQdW(s)\displaystyle\Gamma_t \,=\, \int_{0}^{t} e^{-(t-s) A} Q \,\mathrm{d}W(s) is the pertinent stochastic convolution for ou additive noise, in 2D.

Remark

In 3D, solutions could break down in finite time (we don’t know), and we will need to consider the stochastic analogue of Leray-Hopf weak solutions to send t→+∞t \longrightarrow+\infty.

For the mild formulation, we have the following well-posedness theorem.

Theorem 2 (Almost-sure global well-posedness)

We have that: ℙ-∀Ⅎω∈Ω,∀p≥1,∀T>0,∀γ<α−d2,∀u∈𝑯∩Hγ,\mathbb{P}\,\text{-}\,\forall \hspace{-0.1em} \Finv\, \omega\in\Omega, \quad \forall \,p \,\geqslant\,1, \quad \forall \,T\,>\,0, \quad \forall \,\gamma\,<\,\alpha-\frac{d}{2}, \quad \forall \,u \in \mathbf{H}\cap \mathrm{H}^{\gamma}, there exists a unique solution (ut)(u_{t}) to the mild formulation. Moreover, we have that:

  • (ut)(u_t) is ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t}-adapted,

  • u∈Lp(Ω,𝒞∘([0,T],𝑯∩Hγ))∩L2(Ω,L2((0,T),Hγ+(d−1)))u \in \mathrm{L}^{p}\left(\Omega, \; \mathcal{C}^\circ([0, T], \; \mathbf{H}\cap \mathrm{H}^{\gamma})\right) \;\cap\; \mathrm{L}^{2}\left(\Omega, \; \mathrm{L}^{2}((0, T), \; \mathrm{H}^{\gamma+(d-1)})\right).

  • ∀p≥1,∀β∈(γ,α−d2):\forall \,p \,\geqslant\,1, \quad \forall \,\beta \in (\gamma, \,\alpha-\frac{d}{2})\;: 𝔼W(supt∈[0,T]∥ut∥Hγp)≲T,p,γ1+∥u∥𝑯∩Hγp,𝔼W(∫0T∥us∥Hγ+(d−1)2ds)≲T,δ1+∥u∥Hγ2,𝔼W(supt∈[0,T](tβ−γ2(d−1)∥ut∥Hβ)p)≲p,T,γ,β1+∥u∥Hγp.\begin{align*} \mathbb{E}_{W}\left(\sup_{t\in[0, T]}\left\|u_{t}\right\|_{\mathrm{H}^{\gamma}}^{p}\right) &\underset{T, p, \gamma}{\lesssim} 1+\left\|u\right\|_{\mathbf{H}\cap \mathrm{H}^{\gamma}}^{p}, \\ \mathbb{E}_{W}\left(\int_{0}^{T}\left\|u_{s}\right\|_{\mathrm{H}^{\gamma+(d-1)}}^{2}\,\mathrm{d}s\right) &\underset{T, \delta}{\lesssim} 1+\left\|u\right\|_{\mathrm{H}^{\gamma}}^{2}, \\ \mathbb{E}_{W}\left(\sup_{t \in[0, T]}\left(t^{\frac{\beta-\gamma}{2(d-1)}}\left\|u_{t}\right\|_{\mathrm{H}^{\beta}}\right)^{p}\right) &\underset{p, T, \gamma, \beta}{\lesssim} 1+\left\|u\right\|_{\mathrm{H}^{\gamma}}^{p}. \end{align*}

Proof.

Proof in 2D. The proof is based on mild formulation, regularization of heat semigroup, and properties of stochastic convolution Γt\Gamma_{t}. Estimates on Γt\Gamma_{t} follows from the Factorization Lemma, the Burkholder-Davis-Gundy Inequality, and the smoothing properties of the heat semigroup. ◻

2Random dynamical systems theory

In this paper we formalize the notion of a random dynamical system on a measurable set X\mathrm{X}. An initial motivation for this formalism is to model the iteration of a dynamical system subjected to a random noise. Nevertheless, motivated in particular by fundamental mathematical questions, the general framework has largely deviated from this initial idea and makes it possible to encompass much more varied situations. Let:

  • (T,+)(\mathrm{T},+) be a semi-group,

  • (X,d)(\mathrm{X},d) be a separable, complete and metric space,

  • (Ω,ℱ,ℙ)(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P}) be a probability space such that Ω\Omega is Borel subset of a Polish space and ℱ\mathcal{F} is the set of Borel subsets of Ω\Omega.

2.1. Random dynamical systems

Definition 1

We say that θ:ΩT→ΩT\theta : \Omega^{\mathrm{T}} \longrightarrow\Omega^{\mathrm{T}} is a semiflow on Ω\Omega if:

  • |θ:Ω×T→Ω,(ω,t)↦θtω,\displaystyle\left|\begin{array}{lccl} \theta: & \Omega\times\mathrm{T} & \longrightarrow & \Omega,\\ & (\omega,t) & \longmapsto & \theta^{t} \omega, \end{array}\right. is a measurable mapping,

  • ∀ω∈Ω:θ0ω=ω\forall \,\omega \in \Omega \;:\quad \theta^{0} \omega \,=\, \omega,

  • ∀s,t∈T:θt∘θs=θt+s\forall \,s, t \in\mathrm{T}\;:\quad \theta^{t} \circ \theta^{s}\,=\,\theta^{t + s}.

Definition 2

We say that (θt)(\theta^{t}) is a measure-preserving semiflow on Ω\Omega if (θt)(\theta^{t}) is a semiflow such that: ∀t∈T:(θt)*ℙ=ℙ,\forall \,t\in\mathrm{T}\;:\quad (\theta^{t})^\ast\mathbb{P}\,=\,\mathbb{P}, where f*μ=μ(f−1(⋅))f^\ast\mu\,=\,\mu(f^{-1}(\cdot)). We then call (Ω,ℱ,ℙ,(θt)t∈T)(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P},(\theta^t)_{t\in\mathrm{T}}) a measure-preserving system (or dynamical system, abbreviated DS).

Definition 3

We say that A⊂X\mathrm{A}\subset\mathrm{X} is a full μ\mu-measure set if μ(X∖A)=0\mu(\mathrm{X}\backslash\mathrm{A})\,=\,0.

Notations 3

For a borel positive measure μ\mu on X\mathrm{X} we denote its support as: supp(μ):=⋂Fclosedμ(X∖F)=0F,\mathrm{supp}\,(\mu) \;:= \bigcap_{\substack{\mathrm{F}\;\text{closed}\\\mu(\mathrm{X}\backslash\mathrm{F}) \,=\, 0}} \mathrm{F}, the intersection of all full μ\mu-measure closed sets.

Definition 4

We call random dynamical system (abbreviated RDS) on a measurable space (X,ℬX)(\mathrm{X},\mathcal{B}_\mathrm{X}) over (Ω,ℱ,ℙ,(θt)t)(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P},(\theta^t)_t) a family of mappings (𝒯ω)ω∈Ω(\mathcal{T}_\omega)_{\omega\in\Omega} defined for all ω∈Ω\omega\in\Omega by: 𝒯ω:T×X→X,(t,x)↦𝒯ωt(x),\begin{array}{lccl} \mathcal{T}_\omega : & \mathrm{T}\times\mathrm{X} & \longrightarrow & \mathrm{X},\\ & (t,x) & \longmapsto & \mathcal{T}_\omega^t(x), \end{array} and satisfying:

  • (measurability): 𝒯:Ω×T×X→X,(ω,t,x)↦𝒯ωt(x),is (ℱ⊗ℬT⊗ℬX,ℬX)-mesurable,\begin{array}{lccl} \mathcal{T}: & \Omega\times\mathrm{T}\times\mathrm{X} & \longrightarrow & \mathrm{X},\\ & (\omega,t,x) & \longmapsto & \mathcal{T}_\omega^t(x), \end{array} \;\;\text{is $(\mathcal{F}\otimes\mathcal{B}_\mathrm{T}\otimes\mathcal{B}_\mathrm{X},\,\mathcal{B}_\mathrm{X})$-mesurable},

  • (cocyle property): 𝒯ωt\quad\mathcal{T}_\omega^t form a cocycle over θ\theta ∀ω∈Ω,∀s,t∈T:𝒯ωt+s=𝒯(θsω)t∘𝒯ωs,\forall \,\omega\in\Omega, \quad \forall \,s,t\in\mathrm{T}\;:\quad \mathcal{T}^{t + s}_\omega\,=\,\mathcal{T}^t_{(\theta^s \omega)}\circ\mathcal{T}^s_\omega, and 𝒯ω0=idX\mathcal{T}^0_\omega \,=\, \mathrm{id}_\mathrm{X}\; if 0∈T0\in\mathrm{T} (for all ω∈Ω\omega\in\Omega).

Remark

The composition creates a certain break of symmetry in the theory.

Definition 5

When T=𝒁+\mathrm{T}=\mathbf{Z}_+, the phase 𝒯ωn(x)\mathcal{T}^n_\omega(x) represents the state of the system after nn iterations. In this case, we call discrete time RDS. When T=𝑹+\mathrm{T}=\mathbf{R}_+, the phase 𝒯t(x)\mathcal{T}^t(x) represents the state of the system at time tt from xx at t=0t=0. In this case, we call continuous time RDS.

Smoothness properties

Let 𝒯\mathcal{T} be a RDS on X\mathrm{X}.

Definition 6

𝒯\mathcal{T} is said to be:

  • continuous (or topological) on X\mathrm{X} if for all ω∈Ω:𝒯ωis continuous on T×X\omega\in\Omega \;:\; \mathcal{T}_\omega \;\;\text{is continuous on }\mathrm{T}\times\mathrm{X}.

  • smooth of class 𝒞k\mathcal{C}^k if for all (ω,t)∈Ω×T:𝒯ωt(\omega,t)\in\Omega\times\mathrm{T}\;:\;\mathcal{T}_\omega^t is smooth of class 𝒞k\mathcal{C}^k on X\mathrm{X}.

  • linear if X\mathrm{X} is a finite-dimensional vector space and for all (ω,t)∈Ω×T:𝒯ωt∈ℒ(X)(\omega,t)\in\Omega\times\mathrm{T}\;:\;\mathcal{T}_\omega^t \in \mathcal{L}(\mathrm{X}).

We introduce a stronger definition of continuity for our system as follows.

Notations 4

For metric spaces V,W\mathrm{V},\mathrm{W}, we define the space of strongly continuous maps 𝒞u,b(V,W)\mathcal{C}_{u,b}(\mathrm{V},\mathrm{W}) as the space of continuous function f:V→Wf:\mathrm{V}\longrightarrow\mathrm{W} such that for all B⊂V\mathrm{B}\subset\mathrm{V} bounded:

  • f|Bf_{\vert\mathrm{B}} is uniformly continuous on B\mathrm{B},

  • f(B)f(\mathrm{B}) is bounded.

Hence we say that:

Definition 7

𝒯\mathcal{T} on X\mathrm{X} is strongly continuous on T×X\mathrm{T}\times\mathrm{X} if for all ω∈Ω:𝒯ω∈𝒞u,b(T×X,X)\omega\in\Omega\;:\; \mathcal{T}_\omega \in \mathcal{C}_{u,b}(\mathrm{T}\times\mathrm{X},\mathrm{X}).

Increments condition

For the remainder of our paper, we assume that the semigroup T=𝑹+\mathrm{T}\,=\,\mathbf{R}_+.

Definition 8

For s≤t∈Ts \,\leqslant\,t \in \mathrm{T}, we call a increment the following random variable: 𝒯θs(⋅)t−s:Ω→XX.\mathcal{T}^{t-s}_{\theta^{s}(\cdot)} \;:\; \Omega \;\longrightarrow\; \mathrm{X}^\mathrm{X}.

Definition 9

We say that 𝒯\mathcal{T} has independent increments if: ∀s,t∈T:𝒯ωtis independent of 𝒯θtωs.\forall \,s,t\in\mathrm{T}\;:\quad \mathcal{T}_\omega^t \;\;\text{is independent of } \mathcal{T}^s_{\theta^t\omega}.

Proposition 3 (Characterisation)

𝒯\mathcal{T} has independent increments if and only if: ∀t0≤t1≤…≤tn:𝒯θt0(⋅)t1−t0,𝒯θt1(⋅)t2−t1,…,𝒯θtn−1(⋅)tn−tn−1are independent.\forall \,t_0 \,\leqslant\,t_1 \,\leqslant\,\hdots \,\leqslant\,t_n \;:\quad \mathcal{T}_{\theta^{t_0}(\cdot)}^{t_1-t_0}, \; \mathcal{T}_{\theta^{t_1}(\cdot)}^{t_2-t_1}, \;\hdots\;, \mathcal{T}_{\theta^{t_{n-1}}(\cdot)}^{t_n-t_{n-1}} \;\;\text{are independent}.

Theorem 4 (Stationary increments)

Each RDS with independent increments has stationary increments and: ∀t≥s:ℙ(𝒯θs(⋅)t−s)=ℙ(𝒯(⋅)t−s).\forall \,t\,\geqslant\,s \;:\quad \mathbb{P}_{(\mathcal{T}^{t-s}_{\theta^s(\cdot)})} \,=\, \mathbb{P}_{(\mathcal{T}^{t-s}_{(\cdot)})}. In particular, by the θt\theta^t invariance of ℙ:\mathbb{P}\;: ∀s∈T:𝒯θsωt=𝒯ωt\forall \,s \in \mathrm{T}\;:\quad \mathcal{T}_{\theta^s\omega}^t \,=\, \mathcal{T}_{\omega}^t

Proof.

The θt\theta^t-invariance of ℙ\mathbb{P} implies that the joint distribution of the increments doesn’t change if the tit_i are replaced by ti+t∈Tt_i+t\in\mathrm{T}. ◻

2.2. Markov RDS

Let (xt)t≥0(x_{t})_{t \,\geqslant\,0} be a stochastic process.

Definition 10

Let x∈Xx \in \mathrm{X} be the initial point of (xt)(x_t). We say that (xt)t≥0(x_{t})_{t \,\geqslant\,0} is derived from RDS 𝒯\mathcal{T}, if: {xt=𝒯ωtx0 , x0=x . \begin{cases} x_{t}\,=\,\mathcal{T}_{\omega}^{t} x_{0} \text{ , } \\ x_{0}\,=\,x \text{ . } \end{cases}

Lemma 5

If 𝒯\mathcal{T} is continuous and has independent increments, then (xt)t≥0(x_{t})_{t \,\geqslant\,0} is Markovian.

Proof.

Straightforward. ◻

We extend the transition function of a stochastic process to a RDS:

Definition 11

We associate the Markov semi-group (or Markov kernel) to 𝒯\mathcal{T} as the operators defined for all t∈Tt\in\mathrm{T} as: Pt:X×ℬX→𝑹(x,K)↦ℙ({ω∈Ω:𝒯ωtx∈K}).\begin{array}{lccl} \mathrm{P}_{t}: & \mathrm{X}\times\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{X}} & \longrightarrow & \mathbf{R}\\ & (x, \; \mathrm{K}) & \longmapsto & \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\left\{\omega\in\Omega\;:\;\mathcal{T}_\omega^tx \in \mathrm{K}\right\}\right). \end{array} The Markov property of (xt)(x_{t}) implies the semi-group relation: Ps+t=Pt∘Ps\;\mathrm{P}_{s+t}\,=\,\mathrm{P}_{t} \circ \mathrm{P}_{s}.

Remark

We can rewrite the Markov semi-group as: Pt(x,K)=∫Ω𝟙K(𝒯ωtx)dℙ(ω).\mathrm{P}_t(x,\mathrm{K}) \,=\, \int_\Omega \mathbb{1}_{\mathrm{K}}(\mathcal{T}_\omega^t x) \, \mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}(\omega).

To each Markov kernel there correspond two families of linear operators acting in the spaces of bounded measurable functions L∞(X)\mathrm{L}^{\infty}(\mathrm{X}) and of probability measures 𝒫(X)\mathcal{P}(\mathrm{X}).

Definition 12

The transition operator Pt:L∞(X)→L∞(X)\mathrm{P}_t:\mathrm{L}^\infty(\mathrm{X}) \longrightarrow\mathrm{L}^\infty(\mathrm{X}) of 𝒯\mathcal{T} is defined for all h∈L∞(X,𝑹)h \in \mathrm{L}^\infty(\mathrm{X},\mathbf{R}) by: Pth:X→𝑹x↦∫Xh(y)Pt(x,dy).\begin{array}{lccl} \mathrm{P}_{t} h: & \mathrm{X} & \longrightarrow & \mathbf{R}\\ & x & \longmapsto & \displaystyle\int_\mathrm{X}h(y) \mathrm{P}_{t}(x, \mathrm{d}y). \end{array}

Remark

Note that for all K∈ℬX\mathrm{K}\in\mathcal{B}_\mathrm{X}, we have: Pt𝟙K(x)=∫X𝟙K(y)Pt(x,dy)=∫KPt(x,dy)=Pt(x,K).\mathrm{P}_t \mathbb{1}_\mathrm{K}(x) \,=\, \int_\mathrm{X}\mathbb{1}_\mathrm{K}(y)\mathrm{P}_t(x,\mathrm{d}y) \,=\, \int_\mathrm{K}\mathrm{P}_t(x,\mathrm{d}y) \,=\, \mathrm{P}_t(x,\mathrm{K}).

Proposition 6

We have: Pth(x)=∫Ωh(𝒯ωtx)dℙ(ω).\mathrm{P}_t h(x) \,=\, \int_\Omega h(\mathcal{T}_\omega^t x) \, \mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}(\omega).

Proof.

By the previous remark, for all K∈ℬX\mathrm{K}\in\mathcal{B}_\mathrm{X} we have: Pt𝟙K(x)=Pt(x,K)=∫Ω𝟙K(𝒯ωtx)dℙ(ω).\mathrm{P}_t \mathbb{1}_\mathrm{K}(x) \,=\, \mathrm{P}_t(x,\mathrm{K}) \,=\, \int_\Omega \mathbb{1}_{\mathrm{K}}(\mathcal{T}_\omega^t x) \, \mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}(\omega). By linearity, and then by the Beppo Levi theorem, we conclude that the result holds for all bounded measurable function hh. ◻

Definition 13

We define the dual (Pt*)(\mathrm{P}_{t}^{\ast}) of the operator (Pt)(\mathrm{P}_{t}) on the space of finite signed Borel measures on X\mathrm{X} such as for each μ\mu: Pt*μ:ℬX→𝑹K↦∫XPt(x,K)dμ(x).\begin{array}{lccl} \mathrm{P}_{t}^{\ast} \mu: & \mathcal{B}_\mathrm{X} & \longrightarrow & \mathbf{R}\\ & \mathrm{K} & \longmapsto & \displaystyle\int_\mathrm{X}\mathrm{P}_{t}(x, \mathrm{K}) \,\mathrm{d}\mu(x). \end{array}

Smoothness properties

Definition 14 (Feller property)

We say that (Pt)(\mathrm{P}_t) is Feller if for all t∈Tt \in \mathrm{T}: ∀h∈𝒞b(X,𝑹):Pthis continuous on X.\forall \,h \in \mathcal{C}_b(\mathrm{X},\mathbf{R})\;:\quad \mathrm{P}_{t} h \;\;\text{is continuous on } \mathrm{X}.

Remark

Of course this implies that each Pth\mathrm{P}_t h is defined on X\mathrm{X}.

Definition 15 (Continuity)

We say that the semigroup (Pt)(\mathrm{P}_{t}) is continuous on 𝒞u,b(X,𝑹)\mathcal{C}_{u, b}(\mathrm{X}, \mathbf{R}) if for all h∈𝒞u,b(X,𝑹)h \in \mathcal{C}_{u, b}(\mathrm{X}, \mathbf{R}):

  • ∀t>0:Pth∈𝒞u,b(X,𝑹)\forall \,t\,>\,0\;:\;\mathrm{P}_{t} h \in \mathcal{C}_{u, b}(\mathrm{X}, \mathbf{R}),

  • t≥0↦Ptht\,\geqslant\,0 \longmapsto\mathrm{P}_{t} h is continuous in the topology on 𝒞u,b(X,𝑹)\mathcal{C}_{u, b}(\mathrm{X}, \mathbf{R}).

Proposition 7

Let 𝒯\mathcal{T} be a strongly continuous RDS. Then: 𝒯\mathcal{T} has independent increments ⇒\quad\Longrightarrow\quad (Pt)(\mathrm{P}_{t}) is Feller and continuous on 𝒞u,b(X,𝑹)\mathcal{C}_{u, b}(\mathrm{X}, \mathbf{R}).

Proof.

Straightforward. ◻

2.3. Invariant and stationary measures

Let:

  • (X,d)(\mathrm{X},d) be a separable, complete and metric space,

  • (Ω,ℱ,ℙ,(θt)t∈T)(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P},(\theta^t)_{t\in\mathrm{T}}) be a measure-preserving system,

  • 𝒯\mathcal{T} be a strongly continuous RDS with independent increments and (Pt)(\mathrm{P}_t) its Markov kernel.

Skew product and invariant measures

The Markov chain formulation given above is useful in that it identifies stationary measures, i.e., time-invariant statistics on X\mathrm{X} for the RDS. However, the Markov Kernel loses some structure of the RDS in the sens that: Markov kernel can arise from qualitatively different RDS.

We can encodes the entire RDS by extending θ\theta by 𝒯\mathcal{T} as a single "deterministic", measurable semiflow on the augmented space Ω×X\Omega \times \mathrm{X}:

Definition 16

The skew product associated to 𝒯\mathcal{T} is the mapping Θ:Ω×T×X→Ω×X(ω,t,x)↦Θt(ω,x)=(θtω,𝒯ωtx),\begin{array}{lccl} \Theta: & \Omega \times \mathrm{T}\times \mathrm{X} & \longrightarrow & \Omega \times \mathrm{X}\\ & (\omega, t, x) & \longmapsto & \Theta^{t}(\omega, x)\,=\,(\theta^{t} \omega, \mathcal{T}_{\omega}^{t} x), \end{array} where: ∀t∈T:Θtis a measurable DS on (Ω×X,ℱ⊗ℬX)\forall \,t\in\mathrm{T}\;:\quad \Theta^t \;\;\text{is a measurable DS on } (\Omega\times\mathrm{X}, \; \mathcal{F}\otimes\mathcal{B}_\mathrm{X})

Remark

Conversely, every such measurable skew product DS Θ\Theta defines a cocycle on its xx component, thus a measurable RDS. We can thus use RDS 𝒯\mathcal{T}, cocycle 𝒯\mathcal{T} and skew product Θ\Theta synonymously.

We can thus see that the study of our random dynamical system is reduced to that of the deterministic dynamic system (ΩT×X,ℙ)(\Omega^{\mathrm{T}} \times \mathrm{X}, \mathbb{P}).

Definition 17

We define the dual ((Θt)*)((\Theta^{t})^\ast) of the skew product (Θt)(\Theta^{t}) on the space of finite signed Borel measures on Ω×X\Omega\times\mathrm{X} such as for each η\eta: (Θt)*η=η((Θt)−1(⋅))(\Theta^{t})^\ast\eta \,=\, \eta\left((\Theta^t)^{-1}(\cdot)\right)

The skew product provides us a connection between standard ergodic theory, i.e., the theory of invariant measures for individual mappings of a measurable space, and our present setting of random dynamical systems.

Definition 18

We say that η\eta is a invariant measure on Ω×X\Omega \times \mathrm{X}, if η\eta is a probability measure such that for the semiflow Θ\Theta: ∀t∈T:(Θt)*η=η.\forall \,t \in \mathrm{T} \;:\quad (\Theta^{t})^\ast\eta\,=\,\eta.

Stationary measures

Consider a Borel probability μ\mu on (X,ℬX)(\mathrm{X}, \mathcal{B}_\mathrm{X}) and recall that (Pt)(\mathrm{P}_t) is the Markov kernel of 𝒯\mathcal{T}.

Definition 19

We say that the Borel probability μ\mu on X\mathrm{X} is a stationary measure for 𝒯\mathcal{T} if: ∀t∈T:Pt*μ=μ.\forall \,t \in \mathrm{T}\;:\quad \mathrm{P}_{t}^{\ast} \mu \,=\, \mu.

Proposition 8 (Characterisation)

We have that μ\mu is a stationary measure for 𝒯\mathcal{T} if and only if: ∀f∈L1(μ),f≥0:∫XPtf(x)μ(dx)=∫Xf(x)μ(dx).\forall \,f\in\mathrm{L}^1(\mu), \; f \,\geqslant\,0 \;:\quad \int_\mathrm{X}\mathrm{P}_t f(x) \mu(\mathrm{d}x) \,=\, \int_\mathrm{X}f(x)\mu(\mathrm{d}x).

Lemma 9

Let 𝒯\mathcal{T} be a strongly continuous RDS with independent increments. Then:

  • if X\mathrm{X} is compact, or

  • if there exists a Borel probability μ0\mu_{0} for which the sequence (Pt)*μ0(\mathrm{P}_{t})^{\ast} \mu_{0} is tight,

then 𝒯\mathcal{T} admits at least one stationary measure μ\mu.

Proof.

It’s a consequence of a standard Krylov-Bogoliubov argument. ◻

The following theorem makes this connection between standard ergodic theory and random dynamical systems:

Theorem 10 (Connection between SET and RDS, Ohno [25])

Assume 𝒯\mathcal{T} is a strongly continuous RDS with independent increments. Let μ\mu be a Borel probability measure on X\mathrm{X}. Then: ℙ×μis invariant for (Θt)⇔μis stationary for (Pt).\mathbb{P}\times\mu \;\;\text{is invariant for } (\Theta^{t}) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow\qquad \mu \;\;\text{is stationary for } (\mathrm{P}_{t}).

Proof.

Let t∈Tt\in\mathrm{T} and φ∈L∞(Ω×X)\varphi\in\mathrm{L}^\infty(\Omega\times\mathrm{X}). We denote for all x∈Xx\in\mathrm{X}: φ̂(x):=∫Ωφ(ω,x)dℙ(ω).\widehat{\varphi}(x) \;:=\; \int_\Omega \varphi(\omega,x) \mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}(\omega). Then: 𝔼(Θt)*(ℙ×μ)(φ)=∫φd((Θt)*(ℙ×μ))=∫Ω×Xφ(Θt(ω,x))d(ℙ×μ)(ω,x).\mathbb{E}_{(\Theta^t)^\ast(\mathbb{P}\times\mu)}(\varphi) \,=\, \int \varphi \;\mathrm{d}\left((\Theta^t)^\ast(\mathbb{P}\times\mu)\right) \,=\, \int_{\Omega\times\mathrm{X}} \varphi\left(\Theta^t(\omega,x)\right) \mathrm{d}(\mathbb{P}\times\mu)(\omega,x). However, since 𝒯\mathcal{T} has independent increments we have: ∫X∫Ωφ(θtω,𝒯ωtx)dℙ(ω)dμ(x)=∫X∫Ω(∫Ωφ(ω̃,𝒯ωtx)dℙ(ω̃))dℙ(ω)dμ(x)=∫X(∫Ωφ̂(𝒯ωtx)dℙ(ω))dμ(x).\begin{align*} \int_\mathrm{X}\int_\Omega\; \varphi\left(\theta^t\omega,\mathcal{T}_\omega^t x\right) \mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}(\omega)\mathrm{d}\mu(x) &\,=\, \int_\mathrm{X}\int_\Omega\; \left(\int_\Omega \varphi\left(\tilde{\omega},\mathcal{T}_\omega^t x\right) \mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}(\tilde{\omega})\right) \mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}(\omega)\mathrm{d}\mu(x) \\ &\,=\, \int_\mathrm{X}\left(\int_\Omega\; \widehat{\varphi}(\mathcal{T}_\omega^t x) \mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}(\omega)\right)\mathrm{d}\mu(x). \end{align*} Or the Proposition 6 gives us that: ∫Ωφ̂(𝒯ωtx)dℙ(ω)=Ptφ̂(x).\int_\Omega\; \widehat{\varphi}(\mathcal{T}_\omega^t x) \mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}(\omega) \,=\, \mathrm{P}_t\widehat{\varphi}(x). Thus we have by definition of Ptφ̂\mathrm{P}_t\widehat{\varphi} and integrating with respect to dμ\mathrm{d}\mu: ∫XPtφ̂(x)dμ(x)=∬X×Xφ̂(y)(Pt(x,dy)dμ(x))=∫Xφ̂(y)d(Pt*μ)(y)=𝔼Pt*μ(φ̂).\int_\mathrm{X}\mathrm{P}_t\widehat{\varphi}(x) \mathrm{d}\mu(x) \,=\, \iint_{\mathrm{X}\times\mathrm{X}} \widehat{\varphi}(y) \left(\mathrm{P}_t(x,\mathrm{d}y)\mathrm{d}\mu(x)\right) \,=\, \int_\mathrm{X}\widehat{\varphi}(y) \, \mathrm{d}(\mathrm{P}_t^\ast\mu)(y) \,=\, \mathbb{E}_{\mathrm{P}_t^\ast\mu}(\widehat{\varphi}). Hence we have: ∀φ∈L∞(Ω×X):𝔼(Θt)*(ℙ×μ)(φ)=𝔼Pt*μ(φ̂).\forall \,\varphi\in\mathrm{L}^\infty(\Omega\times\mathrm{X})\;:\quad\mathbb{E}_{(\Theta^t)^\ast(\mathbb{P}\times\mu)}(\varphi) \,=\, \mathbb{E}_{\mathrm{P}_t^\ast\mu}(\widehat{\varphi}). Finally, such that: 𝔼μ(φ̂)=∫Xφ̂(x)dμ(x)=∫X∫Ωφ(ω,x)dℙ(ω)dμ(x)=∫Ω×Xφ(ω,x)d(ℙ×μ)=𝔼ℙ×μ(φ),\mathbb{E}_{\mu}(\widehat{\varphi}) \,=\, \int_\mathrm{X}\widehat{\varphi}(x)\mathrm{d}\mu(x) \,=\, \int_\mathrm{X}\int_\Omega \varphi(\omega,x)\mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}(\omega)\mathrm{d}\mu(x) \,=\, \int_{\Omega\times\mathrm{X}} \varphi(\omega,x) \mathrm{d}(\mathbb{P}\times\mu) \,=\, \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}\times\mu}(\varphi), we have (Pt*μ)=μ(\mathrm{P}_t^\ast\mu)\,=\,\mu if and only if ℙ×μ\mathbb{P}\times\mu is Θ\Theta-invariant. ◻

Ergodic measures

Let μ\mu be a stationary measure for 𝒯\mathcal{T}.

Definition 20

We say that:

  • h∈L∞(X)h\in\mathrm{L}^\infty(\mathrm{X}) is (𝒯,μ)(\mathcal{T},\mu)-invariant function if: ∀t≥0:Pth=hμ-a.s.\forall \,t \,\geqslant\,0 \;:\quad \mathrm{P}_{t}h\,=\,h \quad \;\;\text{$\mu$-a.s}.

  • K⊂X\mathrm{K}\subset \mathrm{X} is (𝒯,μ)(\mathcal{T},\mu)-invariant set if: 𝟙Kis (𝒯,μ)-invariant.\mathbb{1}_{\mathrm{K}} \;\;\text{is $(\mathcal{T}, \mu)$-invariant}.

Definition 21

We say that a stationary measure μ\mu is ergodic if the only (𝒯,μ)(\mathcal{T},\mu)-invariant functions are μ\mu-a.s constant: ∀t≥0:Ptφ=φμ-a.s⇒φ=c∈𝑹μ-a.s.\forall \,t \,\geqslant\,0 \;:\quad \mathrm{P}_{t}\varphi\,=\,\varphi \quad \;\;\text{$\mu$-a.s} \qquad \Longrightarrow\qquad \varphi \,=\, c \in \mathbf{R}\quad \;\;\text{$\mu$-a.s}.

Proposition 11

Let μ\mu be a stationary measure for 𝒯\mathcal{T}. Then: ℙ×μis ergodic for (Θt)⇔μis ergodic for (Pt).\mathbb{P}\times \mu \;\;\text{is ergodic for } (\Theta^t) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad \mu \;\;\text{is ergodic for } (\mathrm{P}_{t}).

Proof.

This proposition is proved in [25]. ◻

3Lyapunov exponent

We introduce the notion of linear cocycle over a given RDS and formulates the Multiplicative Ergodic Theorem (MET) allowing us to define the Lyapunov exponent. Let:

  • (X,d)(\mathrm{X},d) be a separable, complete and metric space,

  • (Ω,ℱ,ℙ,(θt)t∈T)(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P},(\theta^t)_{t\in\mathrm{T}}) be a measure-preserving system,

  • 𝒯\mathcal{T} be a strongly continuous RDS on X\mathrm{X} referred to below as the base RDS, and (Pt)(\mathrm{P}_t) its Markov kernel.

3.1. Materials

Notations 5

For a matrix A∈ℳd(𝑹)A\in\mathcal{M}_d(\mathbf{R}), we write σi(A)\sigma_{i}(A) as the ii-th singular value of AA.

Definition 22

A linear cocycle 𝒜\mathcal{A} over 𝒯\mathcal{T} is a mapping: 𝒜:Ω×T×𝑹d→ℳd(𝑹).\mathcal{A}\;:\; \Omega\times\mathrm{T}\times\mathbf{R}^d \;\;\longrightarrow\;\; \mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbf{R}). with the following properties:

  •  the evaluation mapping Ω×T×X→ℳd(𝑹),(ω,t,x)↦𝒜ω,xt,is ℱ⊗ℬT⊗ℬX-measurable.\begin{array}{lccl} & \Omega \times\mathrm{T}\times \mathrm{X} & \longrightarrow & \mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbf{R}),\\ & (\omega, t, x) & \longmapsto & \mathcal{A}_{\omega, x}^{t}, \end{array} \;\;\text{is $\mathcal{F}\otimes\mathcal{B}_\mathrm{T}\otimes\mathcal{B}_\mathrm{X}$-measurable}.

  •  for fixed ω∈Ω\omega \in \Omega and t≥0t \,\geqslant\,0, the mapping X→ℳd(𝑹)x↦𝒜ω,xtis continuous.\begin{array}{lccl} & \mathrm{X} & \longrightarrow & \mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbf{R})\\ & x & \longmapsto & \mathcal{A}_{\omega, x}^{t} \end{array} \;\;\text{is continuous}.

  •  (cocycle property): ∀x∈X,∀ω∈Ω,∀s,t∈T\quad \forall \,x \in \mathrm{X}, \quad \forall \,\omega \in \Omega, \quad\forall \,s, t \in \mathrm{T}𝒜ω,xt+s=𝒜Θs(ω,x)t𝒜ω,xs\mathcal{A}_{\omega, x}^{t + s}\,=\,\mathcal{A}_{\Theta^{s}(\omega, x)}^{t} \, \mathcal{A}_{\omega, x}^{s} and 𝒜ω,x0=Id\mathcal{A}_{\omega, x}^{0}\,=\,\mathrm{I}_d.

We call the generator of 𝒜\mathcal{A} the mapping: A=𝒜(⋅,⋅)1:Ω×X→ℳd(𝑹)A \,=\, \mathcal{A}_{(\cdot,\cdot)}^1 : \;\Omega\times\mathrm{X}\;\longrightarrow\; \mathcal{M}_d(\mathbf{R}).

Example 1

Let X\mathrm{X} be a Euclidean space and assume that 𝒯\mathcal{T} is 𝒞1\mathcal{C}^{1} on X\mathrm{X}. Then the following 𝒜ω,xt:=Dx𝒯ωt,\mathcal{A}_{\omega, x}^{t} \;:=\; D_{x} \mathcal{T}_{\omega}^{t}, is a linear cocycle and is often referred to as the derivative cocycle for 𝒯\mathcal{T}. Indeed, the cocycle property of 𝒜\mathcal{A} is a manifestation of the Chain Rule from standard calculus and the cocycle property of 𝒯\mathcal{T}.

Definition 23

We say that 𝒜\mathcal{A} is invertible if: ∀ω∈Ω,∀t∈T,∀x∈X:𝒜ω,xt∈GLd(𝑹).\forall \,\omega \in \Omega, \quad \forall \,t \in \mathrm{T}, \quad \forall \,x \in \mathrm{X}\;:\quad \mathcal{A}_{\omega, x}^{t}\in\mathrm{GL}_d(\mathbf{R}).

For a∈𝑹a\in\mathbf{R}, we denote a+:=max⁡(0,a)a^+ \;:=\; \max(0,a).

Definition 24

Assume that, in addition, 𝒯\mathcal{T} has independent increments and admits a stationary measure μ\mu. We then say that the invertible cocycle 𝒜\mathcal{A} is integrable if: 𝔼(∫α+(⋅,x)dμ(x)),𝔼(∫α−(⋅,x)dμ(x))<+∞,\mathbb{E}\left(\int \alpha^{+}(\cdot,x) \,\mathrm{d}\mu(x)\right), \quad \mathbb{E}\left(\int \alpha^{-} (\cdot,x) \, \mathrm{d}\mu(x)\right) \,<\, + \infty, where: α+(ω,x):=sup⁡0≤t≤1log⁡+∥𝒜ω,xt∥andα−(ω,x):=sup⁡0≤t≤1log⁡+∥(𝒜ω,xt)−1∥\displaystyle\quad \alpha^{+}(\omega,x) \;:=\; \sup_{0 \,\leqslant\,t \,\leqslant\,1} \log^{+} \left\|\mathcal{A}_{\omega,x}^t\right\|_{} \qquad\mathrm{and}\qquad\alpha^{-}(\omega,x) \;:=\; \sup_{0 \,\leqslant\,t \,\leqslant\,1} \log^{+}\left\|(\mathcal{A}_{\omega,x}^t)^{-1}\right\|_{}.

3.2. The Subadditive Ergodic Theorem

As a final preparation for the MET, we prove a theorem of Furstenberg and Kesten [17]. We hence need several versions of the latter. We first introduce a generalization of subadditivity to stochastic processes. Let (E,ℰ,ν,(ϑt)t∈T)(\mathrm{E}, \mathcal{E}, \nu,(\vartheta^t)_{t \in \mathrm{T}}) be a metric DS.

Definition 25 (Subadditive Stochastic Process)

A measurable stochastic process (gt(ω))t∈T(g_{t}(\omega))_{t \in \mathrm{T}} with values in 𝑹∪{−∞}\mathbf{R}\cup\{-\infty\} is called subadditive over (E,ℰ,ν,(ϑt))(\mathrm{E}, \mathcal{E}, \nu,(\vartheta^t)) if gs+t(ω)≤gs(ω)+gt(ϑsω)g_{s+t}(\omega) \,\leqslant\,g_{s}(\omega)+g_{t}(\vartheta^s \omega) holds identically. We call gg superadditive if −g-g is subadditive.

Example 2

Let g:E→𝑹g: \mathrm{E}\longrightarrow\mathbf{R} be a measurable function such that t↦g(ϑtω)t \longmapsto g(\vartheta^{t} \omega) is locally integrable. Then St(ω):=∫0tg(ϑsω)ds,S_{t}(\omega) \;:=\; \int_{0}^{t} g(\vartheta^s \omega) \,\mathrm{d}s, is are sub- as well as superadditive.

Theorem 12 (Kingman’s Subadditive Ergodic Theorem, [31])

Let (fn)(f_{n}) be a subadditive sequence of random variables over (E,ℰ,ν,(ϑn)n∈𝑵)(\mathrm{E}, \mathcal{E}, \nu,(\vartheta^{n})_{n \in \mathbf{N}}). Assume f1+∈L1(E,ℰ,ν)f_{1}^{+} \in \mathrm{L}^{1}(\mathrm{E}, \mathcal{E}, \nu) and put m:=inf⁡{1n𝔼(fn),n∈𝑵}.m \;:=\; \inf\left\{\frac{1}{n} \mathbb{E}(f_{n}), \; n \in \mathbf{N}\right\}. Then:

  • there exists:

    • a forward ϑ\vartheta-invariant set U∈ℰ\mathrm{U}\in \mathcal{E} of full ν\nu-measure,

    • a measurable function γ:E→𝑹∪{−∞}\gamma: \mathrm{E}\longrightarrow\mathbf{R}\cup\{-\infty\} with γ+∈L1\gamma^{+} \in \mathrm{L}^{1} such that on U\mathrm{U}:

      • ∀ω∈U:lim⁡n+∞(1nfn(ω))=γ(ω)\displaystyle\forall \,\omega\in\mathrm{U}\;:\quad \lim_{n+\infty}\left(\frac{1}{n} f_{n}(\omega)\right) \;=\; \gamma(\omega),

      • ∀k∈𝑵:γ(ϑkω)=γ(ω)\displaystyle\forall \,k \in \mathbf{N}\;:\quad\gamma(\vartheta^k \omega) \,=\, \gamma(\omega),

      and γ(ω)=m\gamma(\omega)\,=\,m in the ergodic case.

    Further: limn+∞1n𝔼(fn)=m=𝔼(γ)∈𝑹∪{−∞}.\lim _{n + \infty} \,\frac{1}{n} \mathbb{E}(f_{n}) \,=\, m \,=\, \mathbb{E}(\gamma) \;\in\; \mathbf{R}\cup\{-\infty\}.

  • In addition, if: m>−∞and∀n∈𝑵:fn∈L1,m \,>\, -\infty \qquad\mathrm{and}\qquad\forall \,n \in \mathbf{N}\;:\; f_{n} \in \mathrm{L}^{1}, then assertion (a)(a) holds with γ∈L1\gamma \in \mathrm{L}^{1}, and convergence in (i)(i) also holds in L1\mathrm{L}^{1}.

Proof.

We omit the proof as it is easily available in the literature, see e.g. Steele [31]. ◻

Remark

We will use this fundamental theorem with: E=Ω×X,ℰ=ℱ⊗ℬX,ϑ=Θandν=(ℙ×μ).\mathrm{E}\,=\, \Omega\times\mathrm{X}, \qquad \mathcal{E}\,=\, \mathcal{F}\otimes\mathcal{B}_\mathrm{X}, \qquad \vartheta \,=\, \Theta \qquad\mathrm{and}\qquad\nu \,=\, (\mathbb{P}\times\mu).

3.3. The Furstenberg-Kesten Theorem

In 1960, Furstenberg and Kesten proved a Strong Law of Large Numbers for random matrices, with some restrictive positivity conditions on the entries, and without computing the limits explicitly. In 1963, Furstenberg provided a formula for almost sure limits for normalized products of random matrices in terms of a stationary measure. Despite a considerable amount of further work, the invariant (stationary) measures, and hence the limits in the strong law, had not been found explicitly.

Theorem 13 (Furstenberg-Kesten [17])

Assume that, in addition, 𝒯\mathcal{T} has independent increments and admits a stationary measure μ\mu. Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be a linear invertible and integrable cocycle. Then:

  • for each k∈⟦1,d⟧k\in\llbracket 1,d \rrbracket the sequence (ft(k)(ω,x):=log∥∧k𝒜ω,xt∥)t≥0,\left(f_{t}^{(k)}(\omega, x) \;:=\; \log \left\|\wedge^{k} \mathcal{A}_{\omega,x}^t\right\|_{}\right)_{t\,\geqslant\,0}, is subadditive and f1(k)+∈L1(Ω×X,ℱ⊗ℬX,ℙ×μ)f_{1}^{(k)+} \in \mathrm{L}^{1}(\Omega\times\mathrm{X}, \, \mathcal{F}\otimes\mathcal{B}_\mathrm{X}, \, \mathbb{P}\times\mu).

  • there exists:

    • a (Θt)(\Theta^t)-invariant set U∈ℱ⊗ℬX\mathrm{U}{} \in \mathcal{F}\otimes\mathcal{B}_\mathrm{X} of full (ℙ×μ)(\mathbb{P}\times\mu)-measure,

    • measurable functions γ(k):Ω×X→𝑹\gamma^{(k)}: \Omega\times\mathrm{X}\longrightarrow\mathbf{R} with γ(k)+∈L1\gamma^{(k)^{+}} \in \mathrm{L}^{1} such that on U:\mathrm{U}{}:

      • γ(k)(ω,x)=lim⁡t+∞1tlog⁡∥∧k𝒜ω,xt∥\displaystyle\gamma^{(k)}(\omega,x) \,=\, \lim_{t+\infty} \frac{1}{t} \log \left\|\wedge^{k} \mathcal{A}_{\omega,x}^t\right\|_{},

      • γ(k)(Θt(ω,x))=γ(k)(ω,x)\displaystyle\gamma^{(k)}(\Theta^t(\omega,x)) \,=\, \gamma^{(k)}(\omega,x),

      • γ(k+m)(ω,x)≤γ(k)(ω,x)+γ(m)(ω,x)\displaystyle\gamma^{(k+m)}(\omega,x) \,\leqslant\,\gamma^{(k)}(\omega,x)+\gamma^{(m)}(\omega,x),

      and: γ(k)(ω,x)=𝔼(γ(k))\gamma^{(k)}(\omega,x)\,=\,\mathbb{E}(\gamma^{(k)}) in the ergodic case.

Remark (Furstenberg-Kesten Theorem for Other Norms)

We work with the standard scalar product in 𝑹d\mathbf{R}^{d} to define "orthogonal", "singular value decomposition", the corresponding operator matrix norms in ∧k𝑹d\wedge^{k} \mathbf{R}^{d}, etc. However, as all norms in ℳd(𝑹)\mathcal{M}_d(\mathbf{R}) are equivalent, the integrability condition is satisfied or not for all norms simultaneously, and all limits are independent of the norm chosen.

However, the representation 𝔼(γ(k))=infn∈𝑵1n𝔼(log∥∧k𝒜(⋅,⋅)n∥)\mathbb{E}(\gamma^{(k)}) \,=\, \inf_{n \in \mathbf{N}} \frac{1}{n} \mathbb{E}\left(\log\left\|\wedge^{k} \mathcal{A}_{(\cdot,\cdot)}^n\right\|_{}\right) is only valid for so-called matrix norms (i.e., norms on ℳd(𝑹)\mathcal{M}_d(\mathbf{R}) with the additional property ∥AB∥≤∥A∥∥B∥\|A B\| \,\leqslant\,\|A\|\|B\|).

We have limn+∞1nlog⁡|det⁡𝒜(⋅,⋅)n|=γ(d)=∑k=1dχk=𝔼(log|detA(⋅)|∣ℐ)ℙ-a.s.\lim_{n+\infty} \frac{1}{n} \log|\det \mathcal{A}_{(\cdot,\cdot)}^n| \;\,=\,\; \gamma^{(d)} \;\,=\,\; \sum_{k=1}^{d} \chi_{k} \;\,=\,\; \mathbb{E}\left(\log |\det A(\cdot)| \mid \mathcal{I}\right) \quad \mathbb{P}\text{-a.s}. where ℐ⊂ℱ\mathcal{I}\subset \mathcal{F} is the σ\sigma-algebra of θ\theta-invariant sets, and 𝔼(γ(d))=∑k=1d𝔼(χk)=𝔼(log⁡|det⁡A|)∈𝑹∪{−∞}\mathbb{E}(\gamma^{(d)}) \,=\, \sum_{k=1}^{d} \mathbb{E}(\chi_{k}) \,=\, \mathbb{E}(\log |\det A|) \;\in\; \mathbf{R}\cup\{-\infty\} where the expectations are finite when log⁡+∥A±1∥∈L1\log^+\left\|A^{\pm 1}\right\|_{}\in\mathrm{L}^1.

Proof.

By Proposition 57 (iii)(iii): ∥∧d𝒜ω,xn∥=|det⁡𝒜ω,xn|=∏i=0n−1|detA(Θi(ω,x))|.\left\|\wedge^{d} \mathcal{A}_{\omega,x}^n\right\|_{} \,=\, |\det \mathcal{A}_{\omega,x}^n| \,=\, \prod_{i=0}^{n-1}\left|\det A(\Theta^{i}(\omega,x))\right|. We know that 1nlog⁡(⋅)\frac{1}{n} \log (\cdot) of the left-hand side converges on U\mathrm{U}{} to γ(d)=∑k=1dχk=limn+∞1nlog⁡∥∧d𝒜ω,xn∥\gamma^{(d)} \,=\,\sum_{k=1}^{d} \chi_{k} \,=\,\lim_{n+\infty} \frac{1}{n} \log \left\|\wedge^{d} \mathcal{A}_{\omega,x}^n\right\| The (generalized) ergodic theorem applies to the right-hand side since log⁡+|det⁡A|=f1(d)+∈L1\log^{+}|\operatorname{det} A|=f_{1}^{(d)+} \in\mathrm{L}^{1} and yields limn+∞1n∑i=0n−1log⁡|detA(Θi(ω,x))|=𝔼(log⁡|det⁡A(⋅)|∣ℐ)∈𝑹∪{−∞}ℙ-a.s.\lim_{n+\infty} \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \log \left|\det A(\Theta^{i}(\omega,x))\right| \,=\, \mathbb{E}(\log |\det A(\cdot)| \mid \mathcal{I}) \in \mathbf{R}\cup\{-\infty\} \quad \mathbb{P}\text{-a.s}. ◻

Definition of the Lyapunov spectrum

We can now define the main tool for studying Lagrangian chaos. Denote by λ1(ω,x)>…>λp(ω,x)(ω,x)\lambda_{1}(\omega,x)>\ldots>\lambda_{p(\omega,x)}(\omega,x) the different numbers in the sequence χ1(ω,x)≥…≥χd(ω,x)\chi_{1}(\omega,x) \,\geqslant\,\ldots \,\geqslant\,\chi_{d}(\omega,x) and denote by di(ω,x)d_{i}(\omega,x) the frequency of appearance of λi(ω,x)\lambda_{i}(\omega,x) in this sequence.
On the corresponding forward invariant or invariant set U\mathrm{U}{} of full measure the functions p:U→⟦1,d⟧di:{(ω,x)∈U:p(ω,x)≥i}→⟦1,d⟧λi:{(ω,x)∈U:p(ω,x)≥i}→𝑹∪{−∞},\begin{align*} p: &\mathrm{U}{} \longrightarrow\quad \llbracket 1, d \rrbracket \\ d_{i}: &\{(\omega,x) \in \mathrm{U}{}: p(\omega,x) \,\geqslant\,i\} \longrightarrow\quad \llbracket 1, d \rrbracket \\ \lambda_{i}: &\{(\omega,x) \in \mathrm{U}{}: p(\omega,x) \,\geqslant\,i\} \longrightarrow\quad \mathbf{R}\,\cup\,\{-\infty\}, \end{align*} are invariant, and constant in the ergodic case.

Definition 26 (Lyapunov Spectrum)

We then call:

  • the Lyapunov exponents: the functions λi(⋅)\lambda_{i}(\cdot),

  • their multiplicities: the functions di(⋅)d_{i}(\cdot),

  • the Lyapunov spectrum: the set 𝒮(θ,𝒜):={(λi(⋅),di(⋅)),i∈⟦1,p(⋅)⟧}.\mathscr{S}(\theta, \mathcal{A}) \;:=\; \left\{(\lambda_{i}(\cdot), d_{i}(\cdot)), \; i\in\llbracket 1, p(\cdot) \rrbracket\right\}.

Remark

By remark on Furstenberg-Kesten for other norms, the Lyapunov spectrum is independent of the choice of the norm in the space ℳd(𝑹)\mathcal{M}_d(\mathbf{R}). If Θ\Theta is ergodic, we will agree that the Lyapunov spectrum consists of the corresponding set of constants.

3.4. The Multiplicative Ergodic Theorem

Statement of the theorem

Theorem 16 (Multiplicative Ergodic Theorem)

Let:

  • 𝒯\mathcal{T} be a strongly continuous RDS with independent increments, and which admits:

  • μ\mu be a stationary measure for 𝒯\mathcal{T},

  • 𝒜\mathcal{A} be an invertible and integrable linear cocycle.

Then, there exist:

  • a (Θt)(\Theta^t)-invariant set U⊂Ω×X\mathrm{U}{} \subset \Omega \times \mathrm{X} of full (ℙ×μ)(\mathbb{P}\times\mu)-measure,

  • a flag of subspaces for each (ω,x)∈U:(\omega, x) \in \mathrm{U}{}: {0}=:Fp(ω,x)+1⊂Fp(ω,x)(ω,x)⊂⋯⊂F2(ω,x)⊂F1:=𝑹d,\{0\} \;=:\; \mathrm{F}_{p(\omega,x)+1} \;\subset\; \mathrm{F}_{p(\omega,x)}(\omega, x) \;\subset\; \cdots \;\subset\; \mathrm{F}_{2}(\omega, x) \;\subset\; \mathrm{F}_{1} \;:=\; \mathbf{R}^{d},

where dim⁡Fi(ω,x)∈⟦1,d⟧\dim \mathrm{F}_{i}(\omega,x) \in\llbracket 1,d \rrbracket and for which: ∀v∈𝑹d∖{0}:λ(ω,x,v):=limt+∞1tlog⁡∥𝒜ω,xtv∥exists as a limit\forall \,v \in \mathbf{R}^{d} \backslash\{0\} \;:\quad \lambda(\omega, x, v) \;:=\; \lim_{t+\infty} \frac{1}{t} \log \|\mathcal{A}_{\omega,x}^t v\| \;\;\text{exists as a limit} and λ(ω,x,v)=λi(ω,x)⇔v∈Fi(ω,x)∖Fi+1(ω,x).\lambda(\omega, x, v) \,=\, \lambda_{i}(\omega,x) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow\qquad v \in \mathrm{F}_{i}(\omega,x) \backslash \mathrm{F}_{i+1}(\omega,x). Equivalently: Fi(ω,x)={v∈𝑹d:λ(ω,x,v)≤λi(ω,x)}.\mathrm{F}_{i}(\omega,x) \,=\, \left\{v \in \mathbf{R}^{d}: \lambda(\omega, x, v) \,\leqslant\,\lambda_{i}(\omega, x)\right\}. If μ\mu is ergodic, then the function p(⋅)p(\cdot) is constant on U\mathrm{U}{}, and for i∈⟦1,d⟧i\in\llbracket 1, d \rrbracket the functions λi(⋅)\lambda_{i}(\cdot) and di(⋅)d_{i}(\cdot) are constant on {ω∈U:p(ω,x)≥i}\{\omega \in \mathrm{U}{}: p(\omega,x) \,\geqslant\,i\}. Further: ∀i∈⟦1,r⟧,∀v∈Fi(ω,x)∖Fi+1(ω,x):limt+∞1tlog⁡∥𝒜ω,xtv∥=λi.\forall \,i \in \llbracket 1,r \rrbracket, \quad \forall \,v \in \mathrm{F}_{i}(\omega, x) \backslash\mathrm{F}_{i+1}(\omega, x) \;:\quad \lim_{t+\infty} \, \frac{1}{t} \log\left\|\mathcal{A}_{\omega, x}^{t} v\right\|_{} \,=\,\lambda_{i}.

Proof of the MET

We prove the MET for Euclidean spaces. First, we prove the theorem for discrete time. This following lemma is fundamental and we will obtain these stochastic results by exploiting a matrix algebra result.

Then for each v∈𝑹d∖{0}v \in \mathbf{R}^{d} \backslash\{0\} the Lyapunov exponent λ(ω,x,v):=limn+∞1nlog⁡∥𝒜ω,xnv∥\lambda(\omega, x, v) \;:=\; \lim_{n+\infty} \frac{1}{n} \log \|\mathcal{A}_{\omega,x}^n v\| exists as a limit and λ(ω,x,v)=λi(ω,x)⇔v∈Fi(ω,x)∖Fi+1(ω,x),\lambda(\omega, x, v) \,=\, \lambda_{i}(\omega,x) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow\qquad v \in \mathrm{F}_{i}(\omega,x) \backslash \mathrm{F}_{i+1}(\omega,x), equivalently Fi(ω,x)={v∈𝑹d:λ(ω,x,v)≤λi(ω,x)}.\mathrm{F}_{i}(\omega,x) \,=\, \left\{v \in \mathbf{R}^{d}: \lambda(\omega, x, v) \,\leqslant\,\lambda_{i}(\omega, x)\right\}.

    • for all v∈𝑹d∖{0}v \in \mathbf{R}^{d} \backslash\{0\} λ(Θ(ω,x),𝒜ω,x1v)=λ(ω,x,v),\lambda(\Theta(\omega,x), \mathcal{A}_{\omega,x}^1 v) \,=\, \lambda(\omega, x, v), whence ∀i∈{1,…,p(ω,x)}:A(ω,x)Fi(ω,x)⊂Fi(Θ(ω,x)).\forall \,i \in\{1, \ldots, p(\omega,x)\} \;:\quad A(\omega,x) \mathrm{F}_{i}(\omega,x) \subset \mathrm{F}_{i}(\Theta(\omega,x)).

The proof of this lemma follows in a few lines from the Furstenberg-Kesten theorem and the following (deterministic) matrix algebra result called "deterministic MET".

Lemma 18 (Deterministic MET)

Let (An)n∈𝑵(A_{n})_{n \in \mathbf{N}} be a sequence of ℳd(𝑹)\mathcal{M}_d(\mathbf{R}) which satisfies the following two conditions:

Then:

  • the limit lim⁡n+∞(Φn*Φn)1/2n=:Λ≥0\displaystyle\lim_{n+\infty}(\Phi_{n}^{\ast} \Phi_{n})^{1 / 2 n} \;=:\; \Lambda \,\geqslant\,0 exists,

  • the eigenvalues of Λ\Lambda coincide with (eχi)(e^{\chi_{i}}), where the χi\chi_{i} are successively defined by χ1+…+χi=γ(i)\chi_{1}+\ldots+\chi_{i} \:=\; \gamma^{(i)} (put χi=−∞\chi_{i} \,=\,-\infty if γ(i)=−∞\gamma^{(i)} \,=\,-\infty) and satisfy ∀i∈⟦1,d⟧:χi=limn+∞1nlog⁡σi(Φn).\forall \,i \in \llbracket 1, d \rrbracket \;:\quad \chi_{i} \,=\,\lim_{n+\infty} \frac{1}{n} \log\sigma_{i}(\Phi_{n}).

  • let eλp<…<eλ1e^{\lambda_{p}}\,<\,\ldots\,<\,e^{\lambda_{1}} be the different eigenvalues of Λ\Lambda (possibly λp=−∞)\lambda_{p} \,=\, -\infty) and let Ep,…,E1\mathrm{E}_{p}, \ldots, \mathrm{E}_{1} be their corresponding eigenspaces with multiplicities di=dim⁡Eid_{i}\,=\,\dim \mathrm{E}_{i}. Write Fp+1:={0}\mathrm{F}_{p+1} \;:=\; \{0\}, Fi:=⨁i=1pEi,\mathrm{F}_{i} \;:=\; \bigoplus_{i=1}^p \mathrm{E}_{i}, so that Fp⊂…⊂Fi⊂…⊂F1=𝑹d,\mathrm{F}_{p} \subset \ldots \subset \mathrm{F}_{i} \subset \ldots \subset \mathrm{F}_{1} \,=\, \mathbf{R}^{d}, defines a filtration of 𝑹d\mathbf{R}^{d}. Then for each x∈𝑹d∖{0}x \in \mathbf{R}^{d} \backslash\{0\} the Lyapunov exponent λ(x):=limn+∞1nlog⁡∥Φnx∥\lambda(x) \;:=\; \lim_{n+\infty} \frac{1}{n} \log \left\|\Phi_{n} x\right\| exists as a limit and λ(x)=λi⇔x∈Fi∖Fi+1,\lambda(x)\,=\,\lambda_{i} \qquad \Longleftrightarrow\qquad x \in \mathrm{F}_{i} \backslash \mathrm{F}_{i+1}, equivalently Fi={x∈𝑹d:λ(x)≤λi}.\mathrm{F}_{i} \,=\, \left\{x \in \mathbf{R}^{d} \;:\; \lambda(x) \,\leqslant\,\lambda_{i}\right\}.

Proof.

Framework of the proof. This lemma is fully proven in [1]. Let us give the general idea of the proof for the case d=2d\,=\,2.

  • We first consider the singular value decomposition of Φn=VnDnOn\Phi_n\,=\,V_{n} D_{n} O_{n}, where the diagonal matrix is Dn=Diag(σ1(Φn),…,σd(Φn))D_{n}=\text{Diag}(\sigma_{1}(\Phi_{n}), \ldots, \sigma_{d}(\Phi_{n})). By assumption limn+∞Dn1/n=Diag(eχ1,…,eχd).\lim_{n+\infty} D_{n}^{1 / n} \,=\, \text{Diag}(e^{\chi_{1}}, \ldots, e^{\chi_{d}}).

We now show that (both the eigenvalues and) the eigenspaces of (Φn*Φn)12n(\Phi_n^\ast\Phi_n)^{\frac{1}{2n}} converge to limits (eλie^{\lambda_i} and) Ui\mathrm{U}_i.

Finally, the previous convergence has just the right speed to ensure the remainder of the lemma.

The general idea of this particular case allows us to deduce (with harder work) a proof for the general case. ◻

To derive the MET from this lemma, part of the following elementary lemma is needed.

Lemma 19 (Growth of a Stationary Sequence)

Let (E,ℰ,ν,(ϑn)n∈𝑵)(\mathrm{E}, \mathcal{E}, \nu,(\vartheta^n)_{n \in \mathbf{N}}) be a metric DS. Suppose we are given a random variable f:E→𝑹∪{−∞}f: \mathrm{E}\longrightarrow\mathbf{R}\cup\{-\infty\}.

3.5. Particular cases

Projective RDS associated to the cocycle 𝒜\mathcal{A}

Let us write Pd−1\mathrm{P}^{d-1} for the projective space associated to 𝑹d\mathbf{R}^{d}. The action of an invertible matrix A∈GLd(𝑹)A \in \mathrm{GL}_{d}(\mathbf{R}) descends to a well-defined action A:Pd−1→Pd−1.\mathrm{A}: \mathrm{P}^{d-1} \longrightarrow\mathrm{P}^{d-1}. Hence, we can think of the cocycle 𝒜\mathcal{A} as giving rise to an RDS on the product X×Pd−1\mathrm{X}\times \mathrm{P}^{d-1}:

Definition 27

We call projective RDS associated to 𝒜\mathcal{A} every RDS (𝒫ω)ω∈Ω(\mathcal{P}_\omega)_{\omega\in\Omega} defined on X×Pd−1\mathrm{X}\times \mathrm{P}^{d-1} for every ω∈Ω\omega \in \Omega by 𝒫ω:T×(X×Pd−1)→X×Pd−1(t,x,v)↦𝒫ωt(x,v)=(𝒯ωtx,𝒜ω,xtv),\begin{array}{lccl} \mathcal{P}_\omega: & \mathrm{T}\times (\mathrm{X}\times \mathrm{P}^{d-1}) & \longrightarrow & \mathrm{X}\times\mathrm{P}^{d-1}\\ & (t, x, v) & \longmapsto & \mathcal{P}_\omega^t(x,v) \,=\, (\mathcal{T}_{\omega}^{t} x,\,\mathcal{A}_{\omega, x}^{t} v), \end{array}

Proposition 23

Every projective RDS is continuous on X×Pd−1\mathrm{X}\times \mathrm{P}^{d-1}.

Proof.

Straightforward. ◻

The following condition is the independent increments condition for projective RDS:

Definition 28 (Projective independent increments condition)

We say that a projective RDS 𝒫\mathcal{P} have projective independent increments if for all s,t>0s, t\,>\,0: (𝒯.t,𝒜,t)and(𝒯θt.s,𝒜θt.,s)on (Ω,ℱ,ℙ) are independent,(\mathcal{T}_{.}^{t}, \mathcal{A}_{,}^{t}) \quad \text{and} \quad (\mathcal{T}_{\theta^{t} .}^{s}, \mathcal{A}_{\theta^{t} .,}^{s}) \;\;\;\text{on $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})$ are independent}, where the variables are 𝒞u,b(X,X)×𝒞u,b(X,ℳd(𝑹))\mathcal{C}_{u, b}(\mathrm{X}, \mathrm{X}) \times \mathcal{C}_{u, b}(\mathrm{X}, \mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbf{R}))-valued random variables.

Proposition 24

Let 𝒫\mathcal{P} be a projective RDS on X×Pd−1\mathrm{X}\times\mathrm{P}^{d-1} which has projective independent increments. Then, the stochastic process (xt,vt)t∈T(x_{t}, v_{t})_{t \in \mathrm{T}} given by: {(xt,vt)=𝒫ωt(x,v)=(𝒯ωtx,𝒜ω,xtv)(x0,v0)=(x,v)\begin{cases} (x_{t}, v_{t}) \,=\, \mathcal{P}_\omega^t(x,v) \,=\, (\mathcal{T}_{\omega}^{t} x,\,\mathcal{A}_{\omega, x}^{t} v) \\ (x_{0}, v_{0}) \,=\, (x, v) \end{cases} is a Markov process with transition kernel defined for ((x,v),K)∈(X×Pd−1)×ℬ(X×Pd−1)((x, v), \,\mathrm{K})\in(\mathrm{X}\times \mathrm{P}^{d-1}) \times \mathcal{B}_{(\mathrm{X}\times \mathrm{P}^{d-1})} by: P̂t((x,v),K):=ℙ({ω∈Ω:(𝒯ωtx,𝒜ω,xtv)∈K})\widehat{\mathrm{P}}_{t}((x, v), \,\mathrm{K}) \;\;:=\;\; \mathbb{P}\left(\left\{\omega\in\Omega\;:\;(\mathcal{T}_{\omega}^{t} x, \mathcal{A}_{\omega, x}^{t} v) \in \mathrm{K}\right\}\right)

Proof.

Straightforward by Lemma 5. ◻

Proposition 25

The associated skew product semiflow is: τ:Ω×T×X×Pd−1→Ω×X×Pd−1(ω,t,x,v)↦τt(ω,x,v)=(θtω,𝒯ωtx,𝒜ω,xtv).\begin{array}{lccl} \tau: & \Omega \times \mathrm{T}\times \mathrm{X}\times \mathrm{P}^{d-1} & \longrightarrow & \Omega \times \mathrm{X}\times \mathrm{P}^{d-1}\\ & (\omega,t,x,v) & \longmapsto & \tau^t(\omega,x,v)\,=\, (\theta^t\omega, \mathcal{T}^t_\omega x, \mathcal{A}_{\omega,x}^t v). \end{array}

Proof.

Straightforward. ◻

We now turn our attention to the relationship between the ergodic theory of the projective process and the MET. It is not hard to see that any stationary measure ν\nu for (P̂t)(\widehat{\mathrm{P}}_{t}) must project to some (Pt)(\mathrm{P}_{t})-stationary measure μ\mu on the X\mathrm{X}-factor.

Lemma 26

Given a stationary measure μ\mu for (Pt)(\mathrm{P}_{t}), there exists at least one stationary measure ν\nu for the projective semigroup (P̂t)(\widehat{\mathrm{P}}_{t}) such that ν(A×X)=μ(A).\nu(\mathrm{A}\times \mathrm{X}) \,=\, \mu(\mathrm{A}).

Proof.

By Lemma 9. ◻

If ν\nu as above is the unique stationary measure with marginal μ\mu, then we obtain the following refinement of the MET.

Proposition 27 (MET for projective RDS)

Assume that there is only one stationary measure ν\nu for the projective RDS projecting to μ\mu on the X\mathrm{X}-factor. Then, we have that: (ℙ×μ)-∀Ⅎ(ω,x)∈Ω×X,∀v∈𝑹d∖{0}:limt+∞1tlog⁡∥𝒜ω,xtv∥=λ1.(\mathbb{P}\times\mu)\,\text{-}\,\forall \hspace{-0.1em} \Finv\, (\omega,x) \in \Omega\times\mathrm{X}, \quad \forall \,v \in \mathbf{R}^{d} \backslash\{0\} \;:\quad \lim_{t+\infty}\,\frac{1}{t} \log\left\|\mathcal{A}_{\omega, x}^{t} v\right\|_{}\,=\,\lambda_{1}.

Proof.

Straightforward. ◻

Matrix RDS associated to the cocycle 𝒜\mathcal{A}

The cocycle 𝒜\mathcal{A} also gives rise to an RDS on the product space X×ℳd(𝑹)\mathrm{X}\times \mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbf{R}):

Definition 29

We call matrix random dynamical system associated to 𝒜\mathcal{A} every RDS (ℳω)ω∈Ω(\mathcal{M}_\omega)_{\omega\in\Omega} defined on X×ℳd(𝑹)\mathrm{X}\times \mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbf{R}) for all ω∈Ω\omega \in \Omega by ℳω:T×(X×ℳd(𝑹))→X×ℳd(𝑹)(t,x,B)↦ℳωt(x,B)=(𝒯ωtx,𝒜ω,xtB),\begin{array}{lccl} \mathcal{M}_\omega: & \mathrm{T}\times (\mathrm{X}\times \mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbf{R})) & \longrightarrow & \mathrm{X}\times \mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbf{R})\\ & (t, x, B) & \longmapsto & \mathcal{M}_\omega^t(x,B) \,=\, (\mathcal{T}_{\omega}^{t} x,\,\mathcal{A}_{\omega, x}^{t} B), \end{array}

We can similarly define an independent increments condition for matrix RDS and then:

Proposition 28

Let ℳ\mathcal{M} be a matrix RDS on X×ℳd(𝑹)\mathrm{X}\times \mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbf{R}) which has matrix independent increments. Then, the stochastic process (xt,Bt)t∈T(x_{t}, B_{t})_{t \in \mathrm{T}} given by: {(xt,Bt)=𝒫ωt(x,v)=(𝒯ωtx,𝒜ω,xtB)(x0,B0)=(x,B)\begin{cases} (x_{t}, B_{t}) \,=\, \mathcal{P}_\omega^t(x,v) \,=\, (\mathcal{T}_{\omega}^{t} x,\,\mathcal{A}_{\omega, x}^{t} B) \\ (x_{0}, B_{0}) \,=\, (x, B) \end{cases} is a Markov process with transition kernel defined for ((x,B),K)∈(X×ℳd(𝑹))×ℬ(X×ℳd(𝑹))((x, B), \,\mathrm{K})\in(\mathrm{X}\times \mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbf{R})) \times \mathcal{B}_{(\mathrm{X}\times \mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbf{R}))} by: Qt((x,B),K):=ℙ({ω∈Ω:(𝒯ωtx,𝒜ω,xtB)∈K})\mathrm{Q}_{t}((x, B), \,\mathrm{K}) \;\;:=\;\; \mathbb{P}\left(\left\{\omega\in\Omega\;:\;(\mathcal{T}_{\omega}^{t} x, \mathcal{A}_{\omega, x}^{t} B) \in \mathrm{K}\right\}\right)

Proof.

Straightforward. ◻

Remark

Note that if B∈GLd(𝑹)B \in \mathrm{GL}_{d}(\mathbf{R}) and K=K1×K2\mathrm{K}\,=\,\mathrm{K}_{1} \times \mathrm{K}_{2} where K1⊂X\mathrm{K}_{1} \subset \mathrm{X}, K2⊂ℳd(𝑹)\mathrm{K}_{2} \subset \mathcal{M}_{d}(\mathbf{R}), then Qt((x,B),K)=Qt((x,id),K1×(K2B−1)).\mathrm{Q}_{t}((x, B), \mathrm{K}) \,=\, \mathrm{Q}_{t}\left((x, \mathrm{id}),\,\mathrm{K}_{1} \times(\mathrm{K}_{2} B^{-1})\right). Thus, frequently we are only interested in the Markov kernel (Qt)(\mathrm{Q}_{t}) evaluated at (x,id)(x, \mathrm{id}).

Inverse-transpose cocycle associated to the cocycle 𝒜\mathcal{A}

Assume that 𝒜\mathcal{A} is invertible. Another important tool associated to the cocycle 𝒜\mathcal{A} is:

Definition 30

We call the inverse-transpose cocycle associated to 𝒜\mathcal{A}, denoted by (−⊤)(-\top)-cocycle 𝒜\mathcal{A}, the cocycle defined for (ω,t,x)∈Ω×T×X(\omega,t,x)\in\Omega\times\mathrm{T}\times\mathrm{X} by: 𝒜̆ω,xt:=(𝒜ω,xt)−⊤,\breve{\mathcal{A}}_{\omega, x}^{t} \;:=\; \left(\mathcal{A}_{\omega, x}^{t}\right)^{-\top}, where "−⊤-\top" refers to the inverse-transpose of a matrix of GLd(𝑹)\mathrm{GL}_d(\mathbf{R}).

Proposition 29

𝒜̆\breve{\mathcal{A}} is a linear cocycle over the RDS 𝒯\mathcal{T}. Moreover, if 𝒜\mathcal{A} has independent increments or is integrable, then 𝒜̆\breve{\mathcal{A}} has independent increments or is integrable respectively.

Proof.

Straightforward. ◻

Therefore the MET and all the aforementioned material applies, and these objects can be directly represented in terms of the exponents and subspaces of the original cocycle 𝒜\mathcal{A}:

Proposition 30 (Inverse-transpose MET)

Supposed that 𝒯\mathcal{T} has independent increments and 𝒜\mathcal{A} is invertible and integrable. Then 𝒜̆\breve{\mathcal{A}} has Lyapunov exponents λ̆1>⋯>λ̆ř,\breve{\lambda}_{1}\,>\,\cdots\,>\,\breve{\lambda}_{\check{r}}, and associated subspaces F̆2(ω,x),⋯,F̆ř(ω,x)\breve{\mathrm{F}}_{2}(\omega,x), \cdots, \breve{\mathrm{F}}_{\check{r}}(\omega,x) where for almost every (ω,x)∈Ω×X(\omega, x) \in \Omega \times \mathrm{X}: r̆=r,λ̆i=−λr−(i−1)andF̆i(ω,x)=(Fr−(i−1)+1(ω,x))⟂.\breve{r}\,=\,r, \qquad \breve{\lambda}_{i}\,=\,-\lambda_{r-(i-1)} \qquad\mathrm{and}\qquad\breve{\mathrm{F}}_{i}(\omega, x)\,=\,(\mathrm{F}_{r-(i-1)+1}(\omega, x))^{\perp}.

Proof.

This follows on applying the lemma of the MET to the cocycle 𝒜̆\breve{\mathcal{A}} and noting that for all (ω,x)∈Ω×X(\omega,x)\in\Omega\times\mathrm{X} and t∈Tt\in\mathrm{T}: log⁡((𝒜̆ω,xt)⊤𝒜̆ω,xt)=−log⁡((𝒜ω,xt)⊤𝒜ω,xt).\log((\breve{\mathcal{A}}_{\omega,x}^t)^\top\breve{\mathcal{A}}_{\omega,x}^t) \,=\, -\log((\mathcal{A}_{\omega,x}^t)^\top\mathcal{A}_{\omega,x}^t). ◻

Remark

If the cocycle 𝒜\mathcal{A} has projective independent increments, then 𝒜̆\breve{\mathcal{A}} induces the (−⊤)(-\top)-projective process (xt,v̆t)(x_{t}, \breve{v}_{t}) on X×Pd−1\mathrm{X}\times \mathrm{P}^{d-1} defined for fixed initial x0∈Xx_{0} \in \mathrm{X}, v̆0∈Pd−1\breve{v}_{0} \in \mathrm{P}^{d-1} by setting v̆t\breve{v}_{t} to be the projective representative of 𝒜̆ω,x0v̆0\breve{\mathcal{A}}_{\omega, x_{0}} \breve{v}_{0}. Then, all the material from projective process applies with 𝒜̆\breve{\mathcal{A}} replacing 𝒜\mathcal{A} and (xt,v̆t)(x_{t}, \breve{v}_{t}) replacing (xt,vt)(x_{t}, v_{t}). In particular, the conclusions of the proposition related to the MET for projective RDS hold with 𝒜̆\breve{\mathcal{A}} replacing 𝒜\mathcal{A} when the stationary measure for (xt,v̆t)(x_{t}, \breve{v}_{t}) projecting to μ\mu on the X\mathrm{X} factor is unique.

4Positiveness of Lyapunov exponent

This section is fundamental to study the Lagrangian chaos. It is really hard to prove that a system has a positive Lyapunov exponent. For instance, in deterministic systems, it is almost impossible to tell if there’s a exponent even for very simple systems. In the random case, we will use a key idea which comes from RDS with à la Furstenberg rigidity: it says that if you have a volume preserving system, then in order to not being positive you need an almost-surely invariant structure. Hence, we will establish a new refinement of Furstenberg’s criterion. Let:

  • (X,d)(\mathrm{X},d) be a separable, complete and metric space,

  • (Ω,ℱ,ℙ,(θt)t∈T)(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P},(\theta^t)_{t\in\mathrm{T}}) be a measure-preserving system,

  • 𝒯\mathcal{T} be a strongly continuous RDS with independent increments, and which admits:

  • μ\mu be a stationary measure for 𝒯\mathcal{T}.

4.1. Fiber measures

Definition 31

We say that a measure ν\nu is a fiber measure if:

ν\nu is a probability measure on Pd−1\mathrm{P}^{d-1}.

Remark

For a family of fiber measures (νx)(\nu_{x}), we call the fiber measure at xx as the individual measure νx\nu_{x}.

Definition 32

Let A∈ℳd(𝑹)A\in\mathcal{M}_d(\mathbf{R}). We denote the corresponding map on projective space as: A:Pd−1→Pd−1.\mathrm{A}: \mathrm{P}^{d-1}\longrightarrow\mathrm{P}^{d-1}. Let ν\nu be a fiber measure. Then, the pushforward of ν\nu by AA is: A*ν:=ν∘A−1.A_\ast\nu \;:=\; \nu\circ\mathrm{A}^{-1}.

Definition 33

We say that the family of fiber measures (νx)(\nu_{x}) is invariant if: ∀t∈T,(ℙ×μ)-∀Ⅎ(ω,x)∈Ω×X:(𝒜ω,xt)*νx=ν(𝒯ωtx).\forall \,t\in\mathrm{T}, \quad (\mathbb{P}\times\mu)\,\text{-}\,\forall \hspace{-0.1em} \Finv\, (\omega, x) \in \Omega \times \mathrm{X}\;:\quad (\mathcal{A}_{\omega, x}^{t})_{\ast} \nu_{x}\,=\,\nu_{(\mathcal{T}_{\omega}^{t} x)}.

Remark

Hence, a family of fiber measures (νx)(\nu_{x}) is invariant iff for every test function φ∈𝒟(Pd−1)\varphi\in\mathscr{D}(\mathrm{P}^{d-1}): ∫Pd−1φ(s)dν𝒯ω,xt(s)=∫Pd−1φ(𝒜ω,xts)νx(ds).\int_{\mathrm{P}^{d-1}}\varphi(s)\,\mathrm{d}\nu_{\mathcal{T}^t_{\omega,x}}(s) \,=\, \int_{\mathrm{P}^{d-1}}\varphi(\mathcal{A}_{\omega,x}^t s)\nu_{x}(\mathrm{d}s).

4.2. Furstenberg’s criterion

Assume that the stationary measure μ\mu is ergodic and recall that (Θt)(\Theta^t) is a measurable measure-preserving semiflow. Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be invertible, integrable and have independent increments. From the MET, the following limits exists: λ+=limt+∞(1t𝔼(log∥𝒜(⋅,⋅)t∥))andλ−=limt+∞(−1t𝔼(log∥(𝒜(⋅,⋅)t)−1∥)).\lambda_+ \,=\, \lim_{t+\infty} \left(\frac{1}{t}\mathbb{E}\left(\log\left\|\mathcal{A}_{(\cdot,\cdot)}^t\right\|_{}\right)\right) \qquad\mathrm{and}\qquad\lambda_- \,=\, \lim_{t+\infty} \left(-\frac{1}{t}\mathbb{E}\left(\log\left\|(\mathcal{A}_{(\cdot,\cdot)}^t)^{-1}\right\|_{}\right)\right).

Remark

Since for all A∈GLd(𝑹):∥A∥∥A−1∥≥1A\in\mathrm{GL}_d(\mathbf{R}) \;:\; \|A\|\|A^{-1}\| \,\geqslant\,1, we have: λ+≥λ−\lambda_+ \;\,\geqslant\,\; \lambda_-. We want to study under which conditions equality may hold.

Notations 6

Let μ\mu and vv be nonnegative finite (not necessarily probability) measures on some measurable space. We denote dμ/dν\mathrm{d}\mu/\mathrm{d}\nu the density of the absolutely continuous part in the Lebesgue decomposition of μ\mu with respect to ν\nu, that is it’s the ν\nu-a.s. unique function ff such that f(s)=dμdν(s)⇔μ=fν+γ,f(s) \,=\, \frac{\mathrm{d}\mu}{\mathrm{d}\nu}(s) \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \mu\,=\,f\nu+\gamma, with γ\gamma and ν\nu mutually singular. Definition 34

We define the relative entropy of μ\mu with respect to ν\nu by: h(μ∣ν):=−∫log⁡(dμdν(s))dν(s).h(\mu \mid \nu) \;:=\; -\int \log\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}\mu}{\mathrm{d}\nu}(s)\right) \mathrm{d}\nu(s).

Definition 35

We define the entropy of a τ\tau-invariant measure ν\nu by: αν(t):=𝔼(ℙ×μ)[h((𝒜ω,xt)−1ν𝒯ωtx∣νx)].\alpha_\nu(t) \;:=\; \mathbb{E}_{(\mathbb{P}\times\mu)}\left[h\left((\mathcal{A}_{\omega, x}^t)^{-1} \nu_{\mathcal{T}_\omega^t x} \mid \nu_x\right)\right].

Proposition 31

We have αν≥0\alpha_\nu \,\geqslant\,0. Equality αν=0\alpha_\nu \,=\, 0 holds iff for (ℙ×μ)(\mathbb{P}\times\mu)-a.e. (ω,x)(\omega,x): (𝒜ω,xt)*νx=ν(𝒯ωtx)(\mathcal{A}_{\omega,x}^t)_\ast \nu_x \,=\, \nu_{(\mathcal{T}_\omega^t x)}

As (−log⁡)(-\log) is strictly convex, then from Jensen’s inequality: ∫−log⁡(ddνx(𝒜ω,xt)−1ν𝒯ωtx(s))dνx(s)≥−log⁡(∫ddνx(𝒜ω,xt)−1ν𝒯ωtx(s)dνx(s))≥0.\int-\log\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\nu_x}(\mathcal{A}_{\omega, x}^t)^{-1} \nu_{\mathcal{T}_\omega^t x}(s)\right) \mathrm{d}\nu_x(s)\,\geqslant\,-\log\left(\int \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\nu_x}(\mathcal{A}_{\omega, x}^t)^{-1} \nu_{\mathcal{T}_\omega^t x}(s) \mathrm{d}\nu_x(s)\right) \,\geqslant\,0. Moreover, we have: ddνx(𝒜ω,xt)−1ν𝒯ωtxis νx-constant⇔(𝒜ω,xt)−1ν𝒯ωtx=νx⇔ν(𝒯ωtx)=𝒜ω,xt⋅νx.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\nu_x}(\mathcal{A}_{\omega, x}^t)^{-1} \nu_{\mathcal{T}_\omega^t x} \;\;\text{is $\nu_x$-constant} \quad \Longleftrightarrow\quad (\mathcal{A}_{\omega, x}^t)^{-1} \nu_{\mathcal{T}_\omega^t x} \,=\, \nu_x \quad \Longleftrightarrow\quad \nu_{(\mathcal{T}_\omega^t x)} \,=\, \mathcal{A}_{\omega,x}^t \cdot \nu_x. ◻

If λ+=λ−\lambda^{+}\,=\,\lambda^{-}, then:

4.3. A la Furstenberg theorem: classification of invariant fiber measure families

In this section we establish a new refinement of Furstenberg’s criterion which is a classification of the fiber measures (νx)x∈suppμ(\nu_{x})_{x \in \mathrm{supp}\,\mu} comprising a family satisfying the previous topological relation. Leveraging the continuity result, we take advantage of algebraic properties of SLd(𝑹)\mathrm{S}\mathrm{L}_{d}(\mathbf{R}) to obtain a classification for the family (νx)(\nu_{x}) under the assumption that λ+=λ−\lambda^{+}\,=\,\lambda^{-} as in Furstenberg’s criterion.

Continuous dependence of an invariant fiber measure family

First, we establish the continuous dependence of an invariant fiber measure family (νx)(\nu_{x}) on the base point xx under the assumption that the Markov semigroup Pt\mathrm{P}_{t} associated to the RDS 𝒯\mathcal{T} has the strong Feller property.

Definition 36

We say that the Markov semigroup (Pt)(\mathrm{P}_{t}) is:

  • strong Feller if for all t∈T:∀h∈L∞(X,𝑹),Pth∈𝒞b(X,𝑹)t\in\mathrm{T}\;: \quad \forall \,h \in \mathrm{L}^\infty(\mathrm{X},\mathbf{R}), \quad \mathrm{P}_{t}h \in \mathcal{C}_b(\mathrm{X}, \mathbf{R}).

  • ultra Feller if for all t∈T:x↦Pt(x,⋅)is continuoust\in\mathrm{T}\;:\quad x \longmapsto\mathrm{P}_{t}(x, \cdot) \;\;\text{is continuous}, in the total variation distance dTV\mathrm{d}_{TV} on the space of finite signed measures on X\mathrm{X}.

Lemma 36

Assume X\mathrm{X} is a Polish space. Then:

  • Strong Feller on X⇒\mathrm{X}\quad \Longrightarrow\quad Ultra Feller on X\mathrm{X},

  • for all stationary measure μ\mu for (Pt)(\mathrm{P}_{t}) and K⊂X\mathrm{K}\subset \mathrm{X} a Borel set of full μ\mu measure, then: ∀t∈T,∀x∈supp(μ):Pt(x,K)=1.\forall \,t\in\mathrm{T}, \quad \forall \,x \in \mathrm{supp}\,(\mu) \;:\quad \mathrm{P}_{t}(x, \mathrm{K}) \,=\, 1.

Proof.

  • It is sufficient to use the dual representation of the total variation: ∥μ∥TV=sup⁡(∫Xfdμ,f∈𝒞c(X):|f|≤1).\left\|\mu\right\|_{TV} \,=\, \sup\left(\int_\mathrm{X}f \,\mathrm{d}\mu, \; f\in\mathcal{C}_c(\mathrm{X})\;:\;\left|f\right|\,\leqslant\,1\right).

  • First, we check that for all t∈Tt \in \mathrm{T}: {x∈X:Pt(x,K)=1}\left\{x \in \mathrm{X}\;:\; \mathrm{P}_{t}(x, \mathrm{K}) \,=\, 1\right\} is dense in supp(μ)\mathrm{supp}\,(\mu). Hence, the result follows from continuity in total variation.

 ◻

We want to turn the measurable information contained in the Furstenberg’s criterion into topological information. This will be accomplished in two phases: the first step is a continuity result for the invariant measure family (νx)x∈X(\nu_{x})_{x \in \mathrm{X}}:

Proposition 37 (First step)

Assume (Pt)(\mathrm{P}_{t}) is strong Feller, and let (νx)x∈X(\nu_{x})_{x\in\mathrm{X}} be an invariant fiber measure family. Then, there exists an invariant fiber measure family (ν‾x)x∈supp(μ)(\bar{\nu}_{x})_{x \in \mathrm{supp}\,(\mu)} such that:

  • (ν‾x)(\bar{\nu}_{x}) is a μ\mu-a.s version of the original family (νx)(\nu_{x}): μ-∀Ⅎx∈supp(μ):νx=ν‾x.\mu\,\text{-}\,\forall \hspace{-0.1em} \Finv\,\, x \in \mathrm{supp}\,(\mu) \;:\quad \nu_{x} \,=\, \bar{\nu}_{x}.

Statement of the result

Theorem 40 (Classification of invariant fiber measure families [4])

Let d≤3d \,\leqslant\,3 and (ν‾x)x∈supp(μ)(\bar{\nu}_{x})_{x \in \mathrm{supp}\,(\mu)} be the invariant measure family so-obtained. Then, one of the following alternatives holds.

  • For all x∈supp(μ)x \in \mathrm{supp}\,(\mu), there exists an inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩x\left\langle \cdot, \cdot \right\rangle_{x} on 𝑹d\mathbf{R}^{d} such that: x↦⟨⋅,⋅⟩xx\longmapsto\left\langle \cdot,\cdot \right\rangle_x is continuous and, ∀(T,A)∈𝒮,∀x∈supp(μ):Ax:(𝑹d,⟨⋅,⋅⟩x)→(𝑹d,⟨⋅,⋅⟩Tx)is an isometry.\forall \,(T, A) \in \mathcal{S}, \quad \forall \,x \in \mathrm{supp}\,(\mu) \;:\quad A_{x}:(\mathbf{R}^{d},\left\langle \cdot, \cdot \right\rangle_{x}) \;\longrightarrow\; (\mathbf{R}^{d},\left\langle \cdot, \cdot \right\rangle_{T x}) \;\;\text{is an isometry}.

  • There exists p≥1p \,\geqslant\,1, such that for all x∈supp(μ)x \in \mathrm{supp}\,(\mu), there exist proper, distinct, nontrivial linear subspaces Ex1,…,Exp⊊𝑹d\mathrm{E}_{x}^{1}, \hdots, \mathrm{E}_{x}^{p} \subsetneq \mathbf{R}^{d} such that x↦Exix\longmapsto\mathrm{E}_{x}^{i} is measurable and:

    • ν‾x(⋃i=1pExi)=1\displaystyle\bar{\nu}_{x}\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{p} \mathrm{E}_{x}^{i}\right)\,=\,1,

    • ∀(T,A)∈𝒮:AxExi=ETxπ(i),\displaystyle\forall \,(T, A) \in \mathcal{S}\;:\quad A_{x} \mathrm{E}_{x}^{i} \,=\, \mathrm{E}_{T x}^{\pi(i)}, \quad where π=π(T,A)∈𝔖p\pi \,=\, \pi_{(T, A)} \in \mathfrak{S}_p,

    • the collection (Exi)(\mathrm{E}_{x}^{i}) is locally continuous up to re-labelling: there is an open neighborhood U⊂X\mathrm{U}\subset \mathrm{X} of xx and a labelling of the subspaces Exi,x∈U∩supp(μ)\mathrm{E}_{x}^{i}, x \in \mathrm{U}\cap \mathrm{supp}\,(\mu) such that U∩supp(μ)→𝒫(𝑹d)y↦Eyiis continuously varying\begin{array}{lccl} & \mathrm{U}\cap \mathrm{supp}\,(\mu) & \longrightarrow & \mathcal{P}(\mathbf{R}^d)\\ & y & \longmapsto & \mathrm{E}_{y}^{i} \end{array} \;\;\text{is continuously varying}

Remark

The restriction to d≤3d \,\leqslant\,3 is only relevant in case (b). For d≥4d \,\geqslant\,4 the result is likely to be true, but the proof is lengthier due to the fact that among the Exi,x∈supp(μ),1≤i≤p\mathrm{E}_{x}^{i}, x \in \mathrm{supp}\,(\mu), 1 \,\leqslant\,i \,\leqslant\,p there may be arbitrarily many subspaces of dimension ≥2\,\geqslant\,2.

Proof of the classification

Lemma 41 (Baxendale-Furstenberg [3, 16])

Let d≥1d \,\geqslant\,1, η\eta be a Borel measure on Pd−1\mathrm{P}^{d-1} and: H:=Hη:={A∈SLd(𝑹):A*η=η}.\mathrm{H}\;:=\; \mathrm{H}_{\eta} \;:=\; \left\{A \in \mathrm{S}\mathrm{L}_{d}(\mathbf{R}) \;:\; A_{\ast} \eta\,=\,\eta\right\}. Then, H\mathrm{H} is closed and:

    •  ∀i∈⟦1,p⟧\forall \,i\in\llbracket 1,p \rrbracket, there is an inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩i\left\langle \cdot, \cdot \right\rangle^{i} on Ei\mathrm{E}^{i} such that: ∀A∈H,A|Eiis conformal with respect to the inner products ⟨⋅,⋅⟩i,⟨⋅,⋅⟩π(i) respectively.\forall \,A \in \mathrm{H}, \quad A_{\vert \mathrm{E}^{i}} \;\;\text{is conformal with respect to the inner products $\left\langle \cdot, \cdot \right\rangle^{i}, \left\langle \cdot, \cdot \right\rangle^{\pi(i)}$ respectively}.

Proof.

Approximate controllability criteria

Finally, we state a weakening ruling out each alternative in the classification we obtain. Let see a sufficient condition for λ1>0\lambda_{1}\,>\,0 : approximate controllability criteria.

5Lagrangian chaos

5.1. Introduction

We study here the property of chaos (in terms of sensitivity with respect to initial conditions) of a turbulent fluid. Hence, we want to prove that in many circumstances the Lagrangian flow associated to velocity fields are chaotic. To this end, we focus on what happens when particles move together initially: theses two points follow chaotic paths and go off in their own directions.

Statement of the main result

To calculate the mean time before two points of the fluid diverge exponentially, we introduce a precious tool which characterise this property of chaos: the Lyapunov exponent.

Recall that we consider (ut)(u_t) the vector field process on 𝑯\mathbf{H} governed by Systems 1-2. Thus, we study the stochastic flow of diffeomorphisms ϕt:𝕋d→𝕋d\phi^t:\mathbb{T}^d\longrightarrow\mathbb{T}^d, t≥0t\,\geqslant\,0 defined by the random ODE: {dϕtdt(x)=ut(ϕt(x)) , t>0 , ϕ0(x)=x∈𝕋d . \begin{cases} \frac{\mathrm{d}\phi^t}{\mathrm{d}t}(x) \,=\, u_t(\phi^t(x)) \text{ , } & t\,>\,0 \text{ , } \\ \phi^0(x)\,=\,x & \in \mathbb{T}^d \text{ . } \end{cases} This map is random because (ut)(u_t) is random. We then consider the one-point particle motion (xt)(x_t) for all t≥0t\,\geqslant\,0 and x∈𝕋dx\in\mathbb{T}^d by: xt=ϕt(x).x_{t}=\phi^{t}(x). Note that ϕt(x)\phi_t(x) is not a Markov process. In addition, we consider the following Lagrangian process on 𝑯×𝕋d\mathbf{H}\times\mathbb{T}^d: {zt=(ut,xt) , ∀t>0 , z0=(u,x)∈𝑯×𝕋d . \begin{cases} z_{t} \,=\, (u_{t}, x_{t}) \text{ , } & \forall \,t\,>\,0 \text{ , } \\ z_0 \,=\, (u, x) & \in \mathbf{H}\times\mathbb{T}^{d} \text{ . } \end{cases} By the regularity of the velocity fields, the process (zt)(z_t) is as well-posed as (ut)(u_{t}).

Theorem 45 (Positive Lyapunov exponent [4])

Let (ut)(u_t) be governed by the previous system. Then, for all ν>0\nu\,>\,0, there exists a deterministic constant λ+>0\lambda^+\,>\,0 such that for every initial vector field u0∈suppμu_0\in\mathrm{supp}\,\mu and x∈𝕋dx\in\mathbb{T}^d, the following limit exists p.s : λ+=limt+∞1tln⁡|Dxϕt|>0a.s.\lambda^+ \,=\,\; \lim_{t+\infty} \; \frac{1}{t} \ln \left|D_x\phi^t\right| \,>\, 0 \quad \;\;\text{a.s}.

Remark

In particular, every particule in every experiment finally got the same exponent sensibility, and vortices cannot permanently trap any particules.

5.2. Proof of the Lagrangian choas

Outline of the proof. The proof show that, given appropriate ergodic properties of the dynamics, the Lyapunov exponent is strictly positive unless there is a certain p.s invariant certain structure in the motion of xtx_t and its gradient Dx0ϕtD_{x_0}\phi^t.

  • First, we use the MET to prove that the limit defining the Lyapunov exponent λ+\lambda^{+} exists and is constant almost surely.

  • Then, we exclude the invariant structure and deduce the positivity of the Lyapunov exponent by using the classification of fiber measures to prove that this exponent satisfies λ+>0\lambda^{+}>0. Moreover, we need hypoellipticity and approximate controllability arguments to show that: (i)(i) dynamics shows suitable ergodic properties, (ii)(ii) many moves of xtx_t and Dx0ϕtD_{x_0}\phi^t are realized.

RDS framework

Given a random noise path ω∈Ω\omega \in \Omega, a time tt and a fixed initial (u,x)∈𝑯×𝕋d(u, x) \in \mathbf{H}\times \mathbb{T}^{d}, we denote the mapping send (ω,t,u)(\omega, t, u) to the time-tt vector field utu_t conditioned on u0=uu_0\,=\,u: 𝒰ω:T×𝑯→𝑯,(t,u)↦ut.\begin{array}{lccl} \mathcal{U}_\omega: & \mathrm{T}\times\mathbf{H} & \longrightarrow & \mathbf{H},\\ & (t,u) & \longmapsto & u_t. \end{array} We now introduce a random noise path for our one-point motion by an auxiliary process: xt=ϕω,utx,x_t \,=\, \phi_{\omega,u}^t x, which is well-posed. Hypoellipticity: uniqueness of the stationary measure & strong Feller

There have been a number of works proving uniqueness of the stationary measure of the Navier-Stokes equations under degenerate noise. A standard approach is to apply the Khasminskii Theorem: since distinct ergodic stationary measures for strong Feller processes have disjoint supports, we check that there exists a point which belongs to the support of every invariant measure (i.e., weak irreducibility).

Proposition 47 (Strong Feller)

For Systems 1-2, the Markov semigroups associated with (𝒯ω)(\mathcal{T}_\omega), (𝒫ω)(\mathcal{P}_\omega) and (𝒫̌ω)(\check{\mathcal{P}}_\omega) are strong Feller in 𝑯×𝕋d×Pd−1\mathbf{H}\times \mathbb{T}^{d} \times \mathrm{P}^{d-1}.

Proof.

Proved in section 6 of [4]. ◻

To conclude uniqueness of the stationary measures it suffices to prove the following weak irreducibility properties.

Proposition 48 (Weak irreducibility properties)

For systems 1-2 we have the following.

  • The support of any stationary measure for (𝒯ω)(\mathcal{T}_\omega) on 𝑯×𝕋d\mathbf{H}\times\mathbb{T}^d must contain the set {0}×𝕋d\left\{0\right\}\times\mathbb{T}^d.

  • The support of any stationary measure for (𝒫ω)(\mathcal{P}_\omega) and (𝒫̌ω)(\check{\mathcal{P}}_\omega) on 𝑯×𝕋d×Pd−1\mathbf{H}\times\mathbb{T}^d\times\mathrm{P}^{d-1} must contain {0}×𝕋d×Pd−1\left\{0\right\}\times\mathbb{T}^d\times\mathrm{P}^{d-1}.

Proof.

Proved in section 7 of [4]. ◻

Corollary 49

The processes (𝒯ω)(\mathcal{T}_\omega), (𝒫ω)(\mathcal{P}_\omega) and (𝒫̌ω)(\check{\mathcal{P}}_\omega) all have unique stationary measures.

Approximate controllability: Furstenberg’s criterion for infinite-dimensional models

For our infinite-dimensional models, we are not aware of any means by which one can prove a positive density for the conditional law of Dxϕω,utD_{x} \phi_{\omega, u}^{t}. Instead, we are able to prove a certain approximate controllability statement. To articulate this we use the projective process (ut,xt,vt)(u_{t}, x_{t}, v_{t}) on 𝑯×𝕋d×Pd−1\mathbf{H}\times \mathbb{T}^{d} \times \mathrm{P}^{d-1}.

Proposition 50 (Approximate controllability condition)

For any x,y∈𝕋dx, y \in \mathbb{T}^{d} and t>0t\,>\,0, we have the following:

  • for any ε,M>0\varepsilon, M \,>\, 0, we have that ℙ((ut,xt)∈ℬε(0)×ℬε(y),|At|>M∣u0=0,x0=x,A0=id)>0.\mathbb{P}\left((u_{t}, x_{t}) \in \mathcal{B}_{\varepsilon}(0) \times \mathcal{B}_{\varepsilon}(y), \; \left|A_{t}\right| \,>\, M \;\mid\; u_{0}\,=\,0, \; x_{0}\,=\,x, \; A_{0}\,=\,\mathrm{id}\right) \,>\, 0.

  • for any ε>0,v∈Pd−1\varepsilon \,>\, 0, v \in \mathrm{P}^{d-1} and open V⊂Pd−1V \subset \mathrm{P}^{d-1}, we have ℙ((ut,xt)∈ℬε(0)×ℬε(y),vt∈V∣u0=0,x0=x,v0=v)>0.\mathbb{P}\left((u_{t}, x_{t}) \in \mathcal{B}_{\varepsilon}(0) \times \mathcal{B}_{\varepsilon}(y), \; v_{t} \in V \;\mid\; u_{0}\,=\,0, \; x_{0}\,=\,x, \;v_{0}\,=\,v\right) \,>\, 0.

Proof.

Proved in [4]. ◻

End of the proof

Since (𝒯ω)(\mathcal{T}_\omega), (𝒫ω)(\mathcal{P}_\omega) and (𝒫̌ω)(\check{\mathcal{P}}_\omega) have unique stationary measures we then deduce respectively: the almost-sure constancy of λ+\lambda^+ and λ̌+\check{\lambda}^+, the almost-sure growth for (Dxϕt)v(D_x\phi^t)v, and the growth of (Dxϕt)−⊤v(D_x\phi^t)^{-\top} v.

Then, the Strong Feller property proved for (𝒯ω)(\mathcal{T}_\omega) allows us to justify the refinement of Furstenberg’s criterion.

Finally, from the approximate controllability condition we can rule out the refinement of Furstenberg’s criterion for our system, and then complete the proof of Lagrangian chaos.
